name: Classic-Style Test 3
source: Original questions written for LSAT Trainer in the style and difficulty of recent LSATs. Not LSAC material. MIT licensed.

questions.stimulus: Swim coach: Sports scientists warn that teenage swimmers who train more than twenty hours a week face a higher risk of serious shoulder injury than those who train less. But this warning is overblown. Throughout high school I trained more than twenty-five hours a week, often in two sessions a day, and I never injured a shoulder once.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the swim coach's argument is flawed in that the argument
choices: attacks the motives of the sports scientists rather than addressing the evidence on which their warning about injury is based
takes for granted that what is true of competitive swimmers must also be true of athletes in all other sports
fails to consider that the coach may have trained fewer hours in high school than the coach now remembers
treats one person's experience as enough to show that a claim about an increased risk of injury is exaggerated
concludes that heavy training is beneficial merely because it caused no harm in a single case
questions.explanation: A warning about higher risk says injuries are more likely, not certain, so one swimmer who escaped injury does nothing to show the risk is overstated; (D) names this anecdote-versus-general-claim flaw. (C) is tempting but merely possible: nothing suggests the coach misremembers, and accurate memory wouldn't rescue the argument anyway. (E) treats 'not harmful' as 'beneficial,' a conclusion the coach never draws.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The scientists' warning about shoulder injuries in heavy-training teen swimmers is overblown.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The coach trained 25+ hours a week in high school and never hurt a shoulder.

breakdown.analysis: So what if the coach never got hurt? A higher risk means more injuries across many swimmers, not an injury for every single one. This is the anecdote-vs.-general-claim flaw; it's a classic, know it. It's like saying seatbelt warnings are overblown because your cousin never wore one and never got hurt. We need an answer that says the coach uses one case to dismiss a claim about likelihood.

choices.note: The coach never mentions the scientists' motives. Wrong flaw.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: The scientists who issued this warning are paid by a physical therapy company, so we can ignore what they say.

choices.note: There's no jump to other sports anywhere in the argument. Right topic, wrong group.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Heavy training never hurt my shoulders as a swimmer, so it won't hurt the shoulders of pitchers or tennis players either.

choices.note: Tempting, because it hints that the coach's story might be unreliable. But it's merely possible: nothing suggests the coach misremembers, and even with perfect memory one swimmer can't refute a claim about risk.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: I'm sure I studied four hours a night in college, so four hours a night is clearly enough to get top grades.

choices.note: CORRECT. The coach's own injury-free career is the entire evidence, and a risk claim is about how often injuries happen across many swimmers. One case can't show that the risk is exaggerated.
The coach says the warning is overblown, not that heavy training is good for you. 'Didn't hurt' isn't 'helped.' This answer invents a conclusion.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Skipping breakfast never made me sick, so skipping breakfast must be good for your health.

questions.stimulus: Horticulturist: Many gardeners in dry regions spread pale gravel over the soil around their shrubs, believing that the gravel helps the shrubs conserve water. In fact, the practice usually does more harm than good. Pale gravel reflects sunlight onto the shrubs' leaves, raising leaf temperatures, and warmer leaves lose more water than the gravel saves by slowing evaporation from the soil.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the overall conclusion drawn in the horticulturist's argument?
choices: Pale gravel raises the temperature of shrubs' leaves by reflecting sunlight onto them.
As a rule, surrounding shrubs in dry regions with pale gravel hurts those shrubs more than it helps them.
Pale gravel does less to help shrubs in dry regions conserve water than many gardeners believe it does.
Gravel spread over the soil around shrubs slows the evaporation of water from the soil beneath it.
Shrubs whose leaves are warmer lose more water through those leaves than shrubs whose leaves are cooler.
questions.explanation: The claim everything else supports is 'In fact, the practice usually does more harm than good'; (B) restates it in other words. (C) is the near-miss: it says gravel helps less than believed, but the horticulturist claims something stronger, that it does net harm. (A), (D) and (E) are premises.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Spreading pale gravel around shrubs in dry regions usually does more harm than good.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Pale gravel reflects sunlight onto leaves and warms them; warmer leaves lose more water than the gravel saves by slowing soil evaporation.

breakdown.analysis: Ask which statement supports which. The conclusion is the one everything else supports. The first sentence is background: what gardeners believe. 'In fact' flags the author's answer to that belief, and the last sentence explains why. So the conclusion is the 'more harm than good' claim. Watch for an answer that waters it down: 'less help than people think' is not 'more harm than good.'

choices.note: A premise. It's one link in the explanation of why the gravel backfires, not the claim the explanation supports.
CORRECT. 'Hurts more than it helps' is 'does more harm than good,' and 'as a rule' matches 'usually.' Everything else in the argument is offered to support this.

Tempting, because it points the same way as the conclusion. But it's too weak. Helping less than believed is compatible with still helping a little. The horticulturist says the gravel's net effect is harmful.
A premise, and a concession of sorts: the gravel does save some soil water. The argument says that saving is outweighed.
A general fact the argument relies on (warmer leaves lose more water), not the point it's arguing for.

questions.stimulus: Last spring, the Marrow Creek trail, alone among the six trails in a certain nature preserve, had its trailhead signs replaced with new signs asking hikers to stay on marked paths. Over the summer, rangers recorded 40 percent fewer instances of hikers leaving the Marrow Creek trail than they had the summer before. The new signs, therefore, reduced off-trail hiking there.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument?
choices: Hikers interviewed at the Marrow Creek trailhead last summer generally described the new signs as more attractive than the old ones.
Rangers spent fewer hours patrolling the Marrow Creek trail last summer than they had spent patrolling it the summer before.
On the preserve's other five trails, where the signs were not changed, off-trail hiking was about as frequent as the summer before.
A heavy storm closed the Marrow Creek trail for most of July last summer, though the preserve's other trails stayed open.
The new signs were designed by a firm whose signs have been installed in dozens of other parks and nature preserves.
questions.explanation: The argument credits the new signs with a drop in off-trail hiking; (C) shows that on comparable trails without new signs nothing changed, which makes a preserve-wide cause (weather, fewer visitors) less likely. (B) and (D) offer other reasons for fewer recorded incidents, so they weaken; (A) is about how the signs look, not whether they work.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The new signs reduced off-trail hiking on the Marrow Creek trail.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Only Marrow Creek got new signs; recorded off-trail incidents there fell 40 percent from the summer before.

breakdown.analysis: So what if incidents fell? Maybe something else changed that summer: weather, crowds, patrols. We need an answer that rules out an alternative cause or shows the change happened only where the signs went up. The stimulus hands you the comparison group: the five other trails.

choices.note: Tempting, since it's positive about the signs. But liking how a sign looks isn't obeying it. Attractive signs could be ignored just as easily.
This weakens. Fewer patrol hours means fewer chances to record hikers leaving the trail, so the 40 percent drop could be a counting artifact.

CORRECT. The unchanged trails act as a control group. If off-trail hiking held steady there, a preserve-wide cause such as weather or a drop in visitors is unlikely, and the signs look like the difference.
This weakens. If the trail was closed for most of July, there were simply fewer hikers to stray, whatever the signs said.
The designer's track record says nothing about whether these signs changed behavior on this trail. Interesting fact, but not relevant.

questions.stimulus: Two years ago, a certain hospital introduced a checklist that nurses complete with every patient before discharge. Since then, the share of its patients who are readmitted within thirty days of discharge has fallen substantially. Yet the regional health board, which monitors readmissions at every hospital in the region, still describes the hospital's readmission rate as unacceptably high.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above?
choices: Before the checklist, the hospital's readmission rate was nearly double the regional average, and it remains well above that average.
Completing the checklist takes nurses about fifteen minutes for each patient who is discharged from the hospital.
Some of the patients readmitted since the checklist was introduced had been discharged without the checklist being completed.
Administrators at several other hospitals in the region regard the hospital's checklist as a model worth copying in their own wards.
Patients discharged using the checklist report greater satisfaction with their care than patients discharged before the checklist did.
questions.explanation: 'Fallen substantially' is relative to the hospital's own past, while 'unacceptably high' is an absolute judgment; if the rate started at nearly twice the regional average, a big drop can still leave it too high (A). (C) is merely possible and doesn't show why the overall rate is still judged high. (B) and (E) are about time and satisfaction, not the rate.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: the hospital's readmission rate has fallen substantially, but the health board still calls it unacceptably high.

breakdown.analysis: Is a big drop the same as a low rate? No. Watch the switch from a relative word (fallen) to an absolute one (high). If you start very high, you can fall a lot and still be high, like a runner who cuts ten minutes off a marathon and still finishes last. We need an answer that shows the hospital started far enough above the standard that it's still above it.

choices.note: CORRECT. 'Fallen substantially' is measured against the hospital's own past; 'unacceptably high' is measured against a standard. Starting at nearly double the average, the rate can fall a lot and still be too high.
Irrelevant. Nurses' time says nothing about why a falling rate would still be judged too high.
Tempting, because it hints the checklist isn't always used. But it doesn't explain why the board still calls the overall rate too high; we don't know how many such patients there were.
This praises the checklist, which only deepens the puzzle about why the board is unhappy.
Satisfaction isn't readmission. Wrong dimension.

questions.stimulus:
Odile: The Halvard Museum should start charging admission. A modest fee would pay for longer opening hours, and at other museums that introduced such fees, attendance barely changed.

Tomas: Overall attendance might well hold steady. But free admission is what brings in families from the low-income neighborhoods around the museum, and even a modest fee would keep many of them away. The museum should stay free.
questions.stem: Odile and Tomas disagree over whether
choices: the Halvard Museum ought to stop offering free admission and begin charging visitors a modest fee
overall attendance at the Halvard Museum would drop sharply if an admission fee were introduced
a modest fee would change which people visit the museum even if it did not change how many visit
a modest admission fee would bring in enough money to pay for keeping the museum open for longer hours than it is now
the museum's current opening hours are too short to serve the public well
questions.explanation: Odile says the museum should start charging; Tomas says it should stay free, so they disagree over (A). On (B) they agree: Tomas concedes overall attendance might hold steady. (C) is Tomas's point alone; (D) and (E) are Odile's points that Tomas never addresses.

setup.label: Arguments
setup.text: Odile: The museum should charge a modest fee; it would fund longer hours, and attendance barely changed elsewhere.; Tomas: Overall attendance might hold, but a fee would keep low-income local families away, so the museum should stay free.

breakdown.analysis: To disagree, one speaker must say yes and the other no. Odile: charge. Tomas: stay free. That's a direct clash on the policy. Watch Tomas's opening: 'Overall attendance might well hold steady' is a concession, so attendance is not where they split.

choices.note: CORRECT. Odile says the museum 'should start charging admission'; Tomas says 'The museum should stay free.' Yes versus no.

Tempting, because attendance is the topic of Tomas's concession. But that's the point: he concedes overall attendance might hold steady, and Odile says it barely changed elsewhere. They agree, if anything.
Tempting, because Tomas says exactly this. But Odile speaks only to overall attendance; she never says whether the mix of visitors would change. One speaker silent means no disagreement.
Only Odile speaks to this. Tomas never says whether the fee would cover longer hours.
Odile implies she'd like longer hours, but Tomas says nothing about them. One speaker silent means no disagreement.

questions.stimulus: At one software company, no code change is merged into the company's main codebase unless at least one engineer other than its author has reviewed it. Likewise, no change that affects the payment system is merged unless a security lead has approved it. Last week, a change that Imani wrote for the search page was reviewed by a colleague and merged.
questions.stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must also be true?
choices: Imani's change to the search page was approved by a security lead before it was merged into the codebase.
Every change that has been reviewed by an engineer other than its author is eventually merged into the main codebase.
Imani's change to the search page did not affect the company's payment system in any way.
Imani's change to the search page was never examined or approved by any of the company's security leads.
If a merged change never received a security lead's approval, that change leaves the payment system untouched.
questions.explanation: Rule 2: affects payment system → approved by a security lead (if merged). Contrapositive for merged changes: not approved → doesn't affect the payment system, which is (E). We don't know whether Imani's change was approved, so (A), (C) and (D) are all unknown; (B) reverses rule 1.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1. Merged → reviewed by a non-author engineer. 2. Merged and affects payment system → approved by a security lead. 3. Imani's search-page change was reviewed by a colleague and merged.

breakdown.analysis: Hard to prephrase a fact about Imani, because we're never told whether a security lead saw her change. So look for the contrapositive of the rules instead. Rule 2: merged AND affects payments → security approval. Contrapositive: merged AND no security approval → doesn't affect payments. Watch for answers that guess about Imani's change.

choices.note: We don't know this. Approval is required only for payment-system changes, and we aren't told whether Imani's change touched payments.
This reverses rule 1. Review is required for merging; it doesn't guarantee merging.
Tempting: it's a search-page change, so it sounds unrelated to payments. But nothing says a search-page change can't touch the payment system, and nothing says it lacked approval.
We don't know this either. A security lead may well have approved it; the stimulus is simply silent.
CORRECT. This is the contrapositive of rule 2 for merged changes. Any merged payment-system change had approval, so a merged change without approval can't be a payment-system change.

questions.stimulus: The narrator of Corinne Abate's new novel is a nine-year-old girl, yet she tells her story in long, intricately built sentences full of words such as "ineffable" and "penumbra." A narrator's voice is convincing only if it is plausible that someone like the narrator would express herself that way. The novel's narration, therefore, is unconvincing.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the argument?
choices: No nine-year-old has ever used words such as "ineffable" and "penumbra" in describing her own experiences.
The novel does not portray its narrator as so exceptional a child that such language would be believable coming from her.
A novel whose narration is unconvincing cannot succeed as a work of literature, however well it is written.
Most readers of the novel have found the narrator's voice difficult to believe in from the first chapter onward.
Novels narrated by children are convincing only if they are written in short, simple sentences and plain words.
questions.explanation: The test is whether it's plausible that someone like the narrator would talk this way. If the novel presents her as a prodigy, such language could be plausible for her, and the argument collapses; so it must assume she isn't presented that way (B). (A) and (E) are too strong: the argument survives even if a few children use such words or if some long-sentence child narrators work.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The novel's narration is unconvincing.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The nine-year-old narrator uses long, intricate sentences and rare words; a voice is convincing only if it's plausible that someone like the narrator would talk that way.

breakdown.analysis: So she's nine. Is every nine-year-old ordinary? The rule says 'someone like the narrator,' not 'a typical nine-year-old.' If the book makes her a gifted, bookish oddity, the voice might be plausible for her. We need an answer that rules that out: the novel doesn't make her the kind of child who'd talk like this. Negation test for each choice.

choices.note: Too strong. The argument needs this language to be implausible for someone like the narrator, not impossible for every child who ever lived. One precocious child using 'ineffable' doesn't sink the argument.
choices.negation: Some nine-year-old has used words such as 'ineffable' and 'penumbra' about her own experiences. (Argument survives.)

choices.note: CORRECT. Negate it: the novel portrays her as so exceptional that this language is believable from her. Then 'someone like the narrator' would plausibly talk this way, and the conclusion fails.
choices.negation: The novel portrays its narrator as so exceptional a child that such language would be believable coming from her. (Argument collapses.)

choices.note: Adds a consequence the argument never draws. It concludes only that the narration is unconvincing, not anything about the book's success.
choices.negation: A novel with unconvincing narration can still succeed as literature. (No effect.)

choices.note: Irrelevant. The argument applies a standard of plausibility; it doesn't rely on reader reports.
choices.negation: Most readers have not found the voice hard to believe. (The plausibility argument still stands.)

choices.note: Tempting, because it borrows the stimulus's own terms. But it's far too strong. The argument is about this narrator; it doesn't need a rule that every child narrator must write plainly.
choices.negation: Some child-narrated novels with long sentences or unusual words are convincing. (Argument survives.)

questions.stimulus: X-ray images of a portrait long attributed to the workshop of a sixteenth-century painter reveal that the sitter's hand and the angle of her head were repainted several times before the composition was settled. The master's assistants produced copies of his portraits, and an assistant copying a finished painting would have had no reason to alter its composition while working. So the portrait is probably the master's own work rather than an assistant's copy.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?
choices: Several portraits that are known to be the master's own work show no signs of having been repainted beneath their surface.
The master is known to have reworked the poses of the figures in his paintings many times before he was satisfied.
The assistants usually painted their copies from the master's preparatory sketches, which often left the placement of a sitter's hands and head unresolved.
X-ray imaging sometimes fails to detect changes made in paints that contain little or no lead.
Copies made in the workshop were often sold under the master's name, at prices close to those that buyers paid for paintings by the master himself.
questions.explanation: The premise says only that an assistant copying a finished painting would have no reason to revise; the argument takes for granted that the assistants copied finished paintings. If they usually worked from sketches that left the hands and head unresolved, they had to settle those details themselves, so repainting is just what a copy could show (C). (A) is the trap: repainting may be sufficient evidence of the master's hand without being necessary, so unrevised authentic works don't hurt the argument.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The portrait is probably the master's own work, not an assistant's copy.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: X-rays show the hand and head were repainted several times; the assistants copied the master's portraits; an assistant copying a finished painting would have had no reason to change its composition.

breakdown.analysis: Why would revisions point to the master? The premise only covers an assistant copying a finished painting. But who said the assistants worked from finished paintings? That's the gap. An answer saying they copied from something rougher would mean the assistants also had to make choices, and revisions stop being a sign of the master, without denying anything the premises say. Watch for answers that attack the evidence in a way that doesn't matter.

choices.note: Tempting, because it seems to show that revisions aren't a reliable sign. But the argument treats revisions as a sign of the master's hand, not as something every authentic work must have. Authentic works without revisions don't touch it.
This strengthens. A master who habitually reworks poses is just the painter whose canvas would show these changes.

CORRECT. The premise is about copying a finished painting, and the argument quietly assumes that's what the assistants did. If they usually worked from sketches that left the hands and head unresolved, they had to work those out on the canvas, and a copy could show exactly these changes. The premise stays true; the conclusion loses its support.
So? The changes in this portrait were detected. Possible misses elsewhere don't undercut what the X-rays did show.
How copies were sold says nothing about whether this portrait is a copy. Interesting fact, but not relevant.

questions.stimulus: It is widely believed that winter feeding makes birds less able to find natural food. But in a three-year study of black-capped chickadees, birds with access to feeders still got most of their winter food from natural sources, and when the feeders were removed, those birds survived the rest of the winter as well as birds that had never used feeders. Thus, ______.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most logically completes the argument?
choices: chickadees that use feeders in winter may gradually lose at least some of their ability to find food on their own
for chickadees, at least, access to winter feeders does not seem to weaken birds' capacity to feed themselves
winter feeding probably improves chickadees' chances of surviving winters that are unusually long and cold
at least for songbirds, people need not worry about the effects that winter feeding may have on wild birds
for chickadees, at least, natural foods are preferred to the seeds that people offer at feeders
questions.explanation: The study rebuts the dependence worry for chickadees: feeder birds still got most food naturally and survived as well once feeders vanished. (B) draws exactly that limited conclusion. (D) stretches from chickadees and dependence to all songbirds and all effects; (E) turns 'got most food naturally' into a preference; (C) claims a survival benefit the study didn't find.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1. Popular view: winter feeding makes birds dependent and less able to find natural food. 2. Chickadees with feeders got most winter food naturally. 3. When feeders were removed, they survived as well as birds that never used feeders.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Complete the argument after 'Thus.'

breakdown.analysis: The author is pushing back on a popular view, so the blank should say that view doesn't hold, at least where the evidence reaches. The evidence is about one species and about dependence. Watch for answers that stretch either part, and for the trap that repeats the popular view.

choices.note: This repeats the popular view the argument is rebutting. The study found no loss of ability.
CORRECT. It's limited to chickadees and to the ability to feed themselves, which is exactly what the study tested. 'Does not seem to' fits evidence that rebuts rather than proves.
Tempting, since it's hedged. But the study found equal survival, not better survival. No support for a benefit.
Too broad twice over. One species doesn't speak for all songbirds, and dependence isn't every possible effect (disease at feeders, say).
Tempting, since it shares the key's hedge and topic. But getting most food from natural sources isn't preferring it; feeders might simply supply less than the birds need.

questions.stimulus: Last year, judges in one district court granted 40 percent of the requests to postpone a trial that were filed by lawyers from the public defender's office and 60 percent of those filed by private defense lawyers. The public defender's office filed more such requests last year than private defense lawyers did, and no one else filed any.
questions.stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following CANNOT be true?
choices: Judges in that court granted more of the public defender's requests to postpone a trial last year than of the private lawyers' requests.
Last year the district court granted at least half of all the requests to postpone a trial that were filed there.
Most of the postponement requests that the court denied last year had been filed by the public defender's office.
The postponement requests filed by private lawyers last year were, on average, better supported than those of the public defender's office.
Fewer than half of the postponement requests that the court granted last year had been filed by private defense lawyers.
questions.explanation: The overall grant rate is a weighted average of 40 percent and 60 percent, weighted toward the public defender's larger number of requests, so it must be below 50 percent; (B) cannot be true. (A) is the trap: a lower rate on a larger number of requests can still produce more grants.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1. Public defender's requests: 40% granted. 2. Private lawyers' requests: 60% granted. 3. Public defender filed more requests. 4. No one else filed.

breakdown.analysis: Two rates, two group sizes. The overall rate has to land between 40 and 60, closer to whichever group filed more. The public defender filed more, so overall is under 50. Try it: 100 public, 80 private → 40 + 48 = 88 of 180, about 49%. Now look for the answer that says 50% or more. Watch the rate-versus-count trap: a lower rate doesn't mean fewer grants.

choices.note: Tempting, because the public defender's rate is lower. But rate isn't count. With 300 public requests and 50 private ones, that's 120 grants versus 30. Could be true.
CORRECT. The overall rate is a weighted average of 40% and 60%, pulled toward 40% because the public defender filed more. It must be under half, so 'at least half' can't be true.
Could be true; in fact it must be. The public defender's denials are 60% of the larger group; private denials are 40% of the smaller one.
Could be true. The stimulus gives grant rates, not reasons, so better-supported private requests are perfectly consistent with it.
Could be true. If the public defender filed vastly more requests, its 40% could still produce most of the grants.

questions.stimulus: Columnist: As evidence that ranked-choice voting reduces negative campaigning, its supporters point to a city where televised attack ads declined sharply after the system was adopted there. But attack ads declined nationwide that same year, even in cities that kept their old voting systems. So, contrary to what its supporters claim, ranked-choice voting does nothing to curb negative campaigning.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the columnist's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument
choices: confuses a decline that merely coincided with the adoption of a new voting system with a decline that the new system caused
presumes, without providing justification, that televised attack ads are the only form of negative campaigning worth measuring
treats the weakness of the evidence offered for a claim as showing that the claim is false
relies on nationwide figures that may not reflect conditions in the particular city that the supporters cite
concludes that ranked-choice voting is undesirable merely because it fails to achieve one of its intended goals
questions.explanation: The columnist shows the supporters' one example doesn't establish that ranked-choice voting curbs attack ads, then concludes it does nothing to curb them; (C) names that jump from 'not shown' to 'false.' (A) is the trap: it's the supporters' mistake, which the columnist correctly points out, not the columnist's.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Ranked-choice voting does nothing to curb negative campaigning.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The supporters' evidence (one city's drop in attack ads) is matched by a nationwide drop, even where the old system stayed.

breakdown.analysis: The columnist does a good job knocking out the supporters' evidence. But so what? Showing an argument is bad doesn't show its conclusion is false. Ranked-choice voting might still reduce attack ads; we just don't know from this one city. It's like saying: your only witness was lying, so the defendant must be innocent. Absence of evidence isn't evidence of absence; know it. We need an answer that says the columnist treats an unproven claim as a disproven one.

choices.note: Tempting, because this is a real flaw in the story. But it's the supporters' flaw, and the columnist is the one who exposes it with the nationwide comparison. The columnist doesn't commit it.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Attack ads fell the year our city adopted ranked-choice voting, so the new system must have caused the drop.

choices.note: The columnist uses the supporters' own measure; nothing says attack ads are the only form of negativity worth tracking. A real-sounding flaw this argument doesn't commit.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: TV attack ads are down, so negative campaigning is down, never mind the mailers and online posts.

choices.note: CORRECT. 'Your evidence doesn't prove it' becomes 'it's false.' The nationwide drop undercuts the evidence, but it doesn't show ranked-choice voting has no effect at all.
A premise objection. The nationwide figures are used to show the city's drop wasn't unusual, which is a fair use; and even if they were imperfect, that's not where the argument goes wrong.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: National crime fell 5 percent, so crime in our town must have fallen 5 percent too.

choices.note: The columnist never calls the system undesirable. The conclusion is only about negative campaigning. This invents a broader conclusion.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: The new bus lane didn't cut commute times, so the city should never have built it.

questions.stimulus: After a ferry line on a large bay put faster new vessels into service in March, the average time a ferry needed to cross the bay fell by six minutes. Yet in the months since, a larger share of the line's ferries have arrived late at their destination docks than did so in the months before the new vessels entered service.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to explain how the line's ferries could be arriving late more often even though their crossing times have fallen?
choices: Passengers on the new vessels say that the crossing feels noticeably shorter than it did on the old vessels.
Ferries operated by other lines that cross the same bay have also arrived late more often since March.
The new vessels' engines are considerably more powerful than those of the vessels that they replaced.
When the new vessels entered service, the line revised its timetable, reducing the time allotted for each crossing by ten minutes.
Owners of private boats on the bay complain that the larger wakes of the new ferries have made crossing the bay noticeably more difficult and dangerous for them.
questions.explanation: Arriving 'late' is measured against the timetable. If the line cut scheduled crossing times by ten minutes while actual crossings got only six minutes faster, ferries would miss the new schedule more often (D). (C) explains only why crossings are faster, which we already know. (B) gives company but no explanation.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: The new ferries cross six minutes faster on average, but a larger share of ferries now arrive late.

breakdown.analysis: How can faster boats be later? 'Late' is relative to something: the schedule. If the schedule moved more than the boats did, faster boats can still be late. We need an answer that lets both facts be true. Watch for answers that explain only one side.

choices.note: How long the trip feels isn't when the boat arrives. This only echoes the faster-crossing side.

Tempting: maybe something bay-wide (weather, traffic) is causing delays. But a bay-wide delay would also slow crossing times, and crossings got faster. It doesn't explain how this line's ferries are both faster and later.
Explains one side only. More powerful engines account for faster crossings, which the stimulus already tells us. It does nothing to explain the late arrivals.
CORRECT. If the schedule allows ten minutes less per crossing and the boats saved only six, the ferries now run behind schedule more often even though they're faster.
Complaints from private boaters don't bear on whether the ferries arrive on time.

questions.stimulus: Each teacher at Linwood Secondary School spends about an hour a week walking to and from the school's only copy room. The school plans to put a copier in every classroom wing. Teachers will then save that hour, which they can spend helping students, and students' learning will improve.
questions.stem: The answer to which one of the following questions most helps in evaluating the argument?
choices: How much would it cost the school to buy and install a copier in each of its classroom wings?
Would teachers themselves need to spend time loading paper into and clearing jams from the copiers in their wings?
Do teachers at other schools in the district spend more time each week walking to copy rooms?
Is the copy room much farther from some of the school's classroom wings than from others?
Do students at the school currently rate the help they get from their teachers as good or excellent?
questions.explanation: The plan only frees an hour for students if the time saved isn't swallowed by a new chore. If teachers must load and unjam the wing copiers, the gain shrinks or vanishes; if not, the plan looks good (B). (D) reuses the stimulus's setup but doesn't matter, since every wing gets a copier.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Putting a copier in every classroom wing will free teachers' time for students and improve learning.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Each teacher now spends about an hour a week walking to and from the single copy room.

breakdown.analysis: Will the hour really go to students? Copiers don't run themselves. If teachers have to feed paper and clear jams, some or all of the hour is gone again. We need a two-sided question about whether the time saved really becomes student time. Yes on upkeep hurts the plan; no helps it.

choices.note: Cost is a different question. The argument is about whether learning will improve, not whether the plan is affordable.

CORRECT. If teachers must keep the wing copiers running, the saved hour may simply move to a new task, and learning needn't improve. If someone else maintains them, the hour really is freed. Either answer bears on the conclusion.
Other schools are irrelevant. The argument is about what this plan will do here.
Tempting, since walking distance is the heart of the stimulus. But every wing gets its own copier, so it doesn't matter which wings are now farther from the copy room.
The current level of help doesn't tell us whether the plan will raise it. Good help can still get better.

questions.stimulus: Textile cooperative director: We will sell the new Glenmorrow tartan blanket in our shop only if it can be woven entirely from wool produced on our members' farms. The tartan's crimson stripe takes the correct shade of dye only on wool from Kerran sheep, and none of our members raises Kerran sheep. So the Glenmorrow blanket will not be sold in our shop.
questions.stem: The conclusion of the director's argument follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?
choices: The Glenmorrow blanket cannot be woven without a crimson stripe that has taken the correct shade of dye.
If the Glenmorrow blanket could be woven entirely from members' wool, it would be sold in the cooperative's shop.
Some of the cooperative's members could begin raising Kerran sheep within the next few years.
If the cooperative had Kerran wool, it would be able to weave the Glenmorrow blanket with its crimson stripe.
Wool from Kerran sheep costs considerably more than wool from the breeds that the cooperative's members raise.
questions.explanation: The premises show members' wool can't carry a correct-shade crimson stripe, but the conclusion needs that stripe to be required for the blanket; (A) supplies that necessary condition, so the blanket can't be woven entirely from members' wool and won't be sold. (D) is the trap: it gives the sufficient version, which leaves open weaving the blanket without the stripe. (B) reverses the 'only if' rule.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The Glenmorrow blanket will not be sold in the shop.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Sold → woven entirely from members' wool; correct-shade crimson stripe → Kerran wool; no member raises Kerran sheep.

breakdown.analysis: Chain it. Sold → all members' wool. Correct stripe → Kerran wool. Members have no Kerran wool, so members' wool can't give a correct stripe. But who says the blanket needs the correct stripe? That's the gap. Add: blanket → correct stripe. Now: blanket from members' wool → correct stripe → Kerran wool, which members don't have. So no blanket from members' wool, so not sold. We need an answer linking the blanket to the stripe, in the necessary direction.

choices.note: CORRECT. Then the blanket needs a correct-shade stripe, which needs Kerran wool, which no member produces. So it can't be woven entirely from members' wool, and by the rule it won't be sold.
This reverses the 'only if' rule. Knowing when the blanket would be sold doesn't help prove it won't be.
If anything this opens a path to selling the blanket later. It doesn't help prove the conclusion.

Tempting: it links Kerran wool to the blanket. But it's the sufficient version (Kerran wool → can weave). The argument needs the necessary version: no correct stripe → no blanket. This leaves open weaving the blanket some other way.
Cost isn't part of the argument's rule. Irrelevant.

questions.stimulus: Historian: Some scholars argue that the town of Korby must have been poor in the 1600s, because its parish records list very few bequests of silver. But in that period, families who owned silver plate typically gave it to their children while still living, precisely to avoid the heavy tax that was levied on bequests. So the scarcity of recorded bequests may say more about how Korby's wealthy families avoided taxes than about the town's poverty.
questions.stem: The historian's argument proceeds by
choices: arguing that the parish records are unreliable because the officials who compiled them had a stake in the tax on bequests
arguing that the scholars' evidence, properly interpreted, shows that Korby was in fact a wealthy town in the 1600s
granting that the scholars' evidence is accurate but arguing that it is too limited to support any conclusion about the town
proposing a different account of why the evidence that the scholars cite takes the form it does
showing that the scholars' conclusion conflicts with other claims those scholars have made about the town
questions.explanation: The historian accepts that bequests of silver were scarce but says the scarcity may reflect wealthy families giving silver away during their lives to avoid a tax, not poverty: an alternative explanation of the scholars' evidence (D). (B) overstates: the historian says the evidence 'may say more' about tax avoidance, not that it proves Korby was wealthy.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The scarcity of recorded silver bequests may reflect tax avoidance more than poverty.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Scholars: few silver bequests → Korby was poor. Historian: families with silver typically gave it away while living to dodge a heavy bequest tax.

breakdown.analysis: What does the historian do with the scholars' evidence? Doesn't deny it, doesn't add new evidence of wealth. The historian explains the same evidence a different way. That's the classic 'alternative explanation' method. We need an answer that says: offers another account of the evidence. Watch for an answer that turns 'may' into 'shows.'

choices.note: The historian never questions the records' accuracy or the officials' motives. The records are accepted; only their meaning is disputed.

Tempting, because the historian does push the evidence toward wealthy families. But the claim is only that the scarcity 'may say more' about tax avoidance. No conclusion that Korby was wealthy is drawn.

Tempting, since the historian does accept the evidence. But the historian doesn't call it too limited to support anything; the historian says it may support a different conclusion, about tax avoidance by the wealthy.

CORRECT. The scholars read few bequests as poverty; the historian says the same pattern could come from wealthy families giving silver away early to avoid the tax. That's another explanation of why the evidence looks as it does.
The historian doesn't cite any other claims by the scholars, so no inconsistency is shown.

questions.stimulus: Ornithologist: Many pairs of a certain flycatcher species weave a shed snakeskin into the rim of their nest. Since egg-eating rodents tend to avoid anything that smells of snakes, the birds most likely use the skins to keep such rodents away, and not simply because shed skins make good nesting material.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the ornithologist's argument?
choices: Shed snakeskins are lighter, more flexible, and more resistant to water than most other nesting materials available to the birds.
Egg-eating rodents in the flycatchers' range avoid the smell of snakes because snakes there frequently prey on such rodents.
When no snakeskin is available, pairs of the species often weave strips of shiny plastic or foil into their nests instead.
The birds rarely add snakeskin while building the nest itself but often add it within a day or two of laying eggs.
Besides snakeskin, the flycatchers line their nests with feathers and animal fur, materials that are soft and warm.
questions.explanation: If skins were valued as building material, the birds would use them while building. Adding them only once there are eggs to protect ties the habit to egg predators (D). (B) is the trap: it explains a premise the argument already grants (rodents avoid snake smell) without showing that the birds use skins for that reason.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The flycatchers most likely use snakeskins to deter egg-eating rodents, not just as good nest material.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Egg-eating rodents tend to avoid anything that smells of snakes.

breakdown.analysis: So rodents dislike snake smell. Does that show the birds use skins because of it? No. Skins could deter rodents as a side effect while the birds pick them for being light and sturdy. We need something that ties the birds' behavior to the threat to eggs, or that is hard to explain if the skins are just good material. Timing can do that: when do the skins go in?

choices.note: This supports the rival explanation: skins really are good material, so the birds could use them for that alone. If anything it weakens.
Tempting, because it backs up the argument's premise. But the argument already grants that rodents avoid snake smell. Explaining why adds nothing about why the birds use the skins.
This weakens. If the birds substitute shiny plastic, they may be after appearance or texture, not snake scent.

CORRECT. Building material is needed while the nest is being built. A skin that shows up only once eggs are present fits a defense of eggs and fits poorly with 'just good material.' It looks odd at first, but it separates the two explanations.
Other lining materials tell us nothing about why the skins are there. They don't favor either explanation.

questions.stimulus: Urban ecologist: The city plans to line its new boulevards exclusively with fast-growing poplars so that the streets will be shaded within a few years. The city would do better to plant oaks. Admittedly, oaks would take far longer to provide much shade. But poplars are short-lived, and their brittle limbs often break in storms, so the city would likely have to replace most of the poplars within twenty years, just when oaks would be reaching full size.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the role played in the ecologist's argument by the claim that the city would likely have to replace most of the poplars within twenty years?
choices: It is the overall conclusion of the argument, and it is supported by the claims about the poplars' short lives and brittle limbs.
It is a consideration that the ecologist acknowledges tells against the course of action that the argument recommends.
It is supported by other claims in the argument and is in turn used to support a claim stated earlier in the argument.
It is a premise offered in support of the claim that oaks would take far longer than poplars to provide much shade.
It is offered in support of the argument's overall conclusion, and no other claim in the argument is offered in support of it.
questions.explanation: The main conclusion is the unflagged recommendation 'The city would do better to plant oaks'; the replacement claim is drawn from the facts about poplars' short lives and brittle limbs ('so') and in turn supports that earlier recommendation, so it is a subsidiary conclusion (C). (A) is the trap: the claim comes last and follows 'so,' but it is offered as a reason to plant oaks, so it can't be the overall conclusion. (B) mislocates the concession, which is about oaks being slow. (E) gets only half the relation: the claim supports the conclusion, but it is also supported.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The city would do better to plant oaks than poplars.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Poplars are short-lived and brittle → the city would likely have to replace most of them within twenty years (the claim in question), just as oaks reach full size; concession: oaks are slower to give shade.

breakdown.analysis: Where's the conclusion? Not at the end. Ask which statement supports which; the conclusion is the one everything else supports. 1. Poplars are short-lived and brittle. → 2. The city would have to replace most of them within twenty years. → 3. The city would do better to plant oaks. The first sentence is background, and the 'Admittedly' sentence is a concession against 3. So the claim in question is supported (by 1) and supports something (3): a subsidiary conclusion. Most students pick (A) because the claim comes last and follows 'so.' But 'so' only shows the claim is drawn from something; it doesn't show that nothing further rests on it. Here it is the reason oaks are the better choice. We need an answer that says: supported, and in turn supports a claim made earlier.

choices.note: Tempting. It's the last sentence and it follows 'so,' which looks like a conclusion flag. But it's offered as a reason for 'The city would do better to plant oaks.' A claim that supports another claim isn't the overall conclusion.

Wrong concession. The ecologist does concede something, but it's that oaks are slow to give shade. The replacement claim counts against poplars, which helps the recommendation instead of telling against it.

CORRECT. It's supported by the facts about short lives and brittle limbs ('so'), and it supports the recommendation to plant oaks, which comes earlier in the argument. That's a subsidiary conclusion, described abstractly.
Right role word, wrong relation. The claim that oaks are slow is a concession, and nothing is offered to support it; the replacement claim supports the recommendation instead.

Half right, which makes it the strongest trap. The claim does support the recommendation to plant oaks. But it is itself supported: 'poplars are short-lived, and their brittle limbs often break in storms, so…' A claim with support behind it isn't a bare premise.

questions.stimulus: Last season, runners on the Westfield High track team who attended the coach's optional sessions reviewing race footage cut their race times by more, on average, than did runners who skipped the sessions. So, to improve the team's race times this season, the coach plans to require every runner on the team to attend the film sessions.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the argument depends?
choices: Runners who chose to attend the sessions last season were, as a group, no more motivated to improve than the runners who skipped them.
Every runner who attended the sessions last season cut his or her race times by more than every runner who skipped them.
Requiring attendance will not make the sessions any less useful to the runners who already attend them voluntarily.
Requiring every runner on the team to attend the sessions will improve the race times of each runner on the team.
Attending the sessions would help at least some of the runners who would otherwise skip them to run faster.
questions.explanation: The plan improves team times only if making the skippers attend helps at least some of them; negate (E) and requiring attendance changes nothing (E). (A) is the trap: ruling out self-selection by motivation would strengthen the argument, but it isn't required, because the sessions could help even if attendees were also more motivated.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Requiring every runner to attend the film sessions will improve the team's race times.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Last season, runners who attended the optional sessions improved more, on average, than runners who skipped them.

breakdown.analysis: Who is the plan for? The runners who used to skip. The voluntary attendees were already going. So the plan only works if the sessions would actually help some of those skippers. Negate it: the sessions would help none of them. Then the requirement changes nothing. Note the tempting move: the classic self-selection worry (attendees were more motivated). Ruling that out helps the argument, but the argument doesn't need it fully ruled out.

choices.note: Tempting, because self-selection is the obvious gap and this closes it. But it isn't required. Attendees could have been more motivated and the sessions could still help. Negated, the argument is weakened, not wrecked.
choices.negation: Attendees were, as a group, more motivated than skippers. (The sessions might still help; argument survives.)

choices.note: Too strong. An average difference is enough. The argument doesn't need every attendee to beat every skipper.
choices.negation: Some runner who skipped improved more than some runner who attended. (No damage.)

choices.note: Not required. Even if the sessions became a bit less useful for the old attendees, adding the skippers could still improve team times overall.
choices.negation: Requiring attendance will make the sessions somewhat less useful to voluntary attendees. (The plan can still work.)

choices.note: Too strong. The plan aims to improve the team's times, which can happen even if some runners don't improve.
choices.negation: Some runner's times won't improve. (Team times can still improve.)

choices.note: CORRECT. The plan's only new effect is on runners who'd otherwise skip. If attending would help none of them, the requirement can't improve the team's times.
choices.negation: Attending would help none of the runners who would otherwise skip. (Plan accomplishes nothing; argument collapses.)

questions.stimulus: Engineer: Stone arch bridges built in one region during the 1700s are, on average, in noticeably better structural condition today than those built there in the early 1900s. Yet the two groups of bridges now carry similar amounts of traffic, and the older bridges have had nearly two more centuries in which to deteriorate. So that region's eighteenth-century bridge builders followed sounder construction practices than did their twentieth-century successors.
questions.stem: The engineer's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it
choices: fails to consider that builders in the earlier period may have constructed far fewer bridges than later builders did
draws a general conclusion about construction practices from the condition of the bridges in a single region only
takes for granted that the builders of the 1700s had access to the same materials and tools as their successors
takes for granted that the bridges still available for comparison today represent the building work of each period equally well
treats the age of a bridge as though it were the main factor determining that bridge's present condition
questions.explanation: Badly built 1700s bridges have had two centuries to collapse or be torn down, so the ones still standing are likely the best of their era, while early-1900s bridges, good and bad, mostly survive. The argument treats the survivors as a fair sample of each period (D). (A) is the near-miss: how many bridges were built doesn't matter; what matters is which ones survived.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: the region's 1700s bridge builders used sounder construction practices than their early-1900s successors.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Surviving 1700s stone bridges are in better shape than early-1900s ones, despite similar traffic and two extra centuries of wear.

breakdown.analysis: Which 1700s bridges are we looking at? Only the ones still standing. The weak ones probably fell down or were replaced long ago. The 1900s bridges haven't had time to be weeded out. That's survivorship bias: comparing the survivors of a long filter with a group that hasn't been filtered. It's a classic; know it. We need an answer that says the surviving bridges might not represent each period equally.

choices.note: Tempting, because it's about which bridges exist. But the raw number built doesn't matter. Even if the 1700s builders built just as many, the bad ones would have been weeded out. The issue is which survived, not how many were made.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Our school has more trophies from the 1990s than the 1950s, so students were better then, ignoring that the school was twice as big.

choices.note: The conclusion is only about the region's builders, so the evidence and the conclusion cover the same region. No overreach here.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Bridges in the region are well built, so 1700s builders everywhere were skilled.

choices.note: The argument doesn't need this. Better practices could include choosing better materials; nothing in the reasoning depends on equal access.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Old builders made sturdier bridges, so they must have been more skilled, ignoring that they had better stone to work with.

choices.note: CORRECT. The standing 1700s bridges have survived two centuries of weeding out; the early-1900s ones haven't. So the comparison pits the best of one era against a fuller cross-section of another.
The argument treats age as working against the older bridges, then says their better condition is surprising. It doesn't claim age is the main factor in condition.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: That bridge is old, so it must be in worse shape than this new one.

questions.stimulus: In laboratory experiments, yeast cells exposed to mild heat for an hour later survived a severe heat shock far more often than yeast cells that had not been exposed. When a drug that blocks the making of new proteins was given during the hour of mild heat, this protective effect disappeared. When the same drug was given only during the severe heat shock, it had no effect on survival.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the information above?
choices: Yeast cells that make new proteins during a severe heat shock survive the shock more often than cells that do not make them.
The protection that mild heat gives yeast comes from something the cells produce in response to it, not from the exposure alone.
Blocking protein production during mild heat leaves yeast cells less able to survive a severe heat shock than unexposed cells.
Mild heat causes yeast cells to make kinds of proteins that the cells would never produce under any other conditions.
Yeast cells that have been exposed to mild heat for an hour grow more slowly afterward than cells that have not been exposed.
questions.explanation: Blocking protein production during the mild heat cancels the protection, while blocking it during the shock does nothing; so the protection depends on what the cells make while mildly heated, not on the heat exposure by itself (B). (C) is the trap: the effect 'disappeared,' which means survival fell back to the unexposed level, not below it. (A) is contradicted, because the drug during the shock had no effect.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1. Mild heat first → much better survival of a severe shock. 2. Protein-blocking drug during the mild heat → the protection disappears. 3. The same drug during the shock only → no effect on survival.

breakdown.analysis: Hard to prephrase, so work through the controls. Fact 2 says the protection needs new proteins made during the mild heat. Fact 3 says making proteins during the shock doesn't matter. So exposure alone isn't enough; the cells have to build something in response. Watch for answers that misplace the timing, and for 'disappeared' read as 'got worse.'

choices.note: Contradicted. Blocking protein production during the shock had no effect on survival, so new proteins made then don't help.

CORRECT. Mild heat without new protein production gave no protection, so being exposed isn't what protects the cells. Something they make in response is. The answer looks vague, but that's all the experiment shows, and it shows it well.
Tempting, because the drug undoes the benefit. But 'the protective effect disappeared' means survival dropped back to roughly the unexposed rate. Nothing says it fell below that.
Too strong. The proteins needed could be ones the cells make in other conditions too. 'Never under any other conditions' goes far beyond the data.
New information. The experiments measured survival, not growth.

questions.stimulus: Editor: Our newspaper ordinarily keeps its promise to protect the identity of a source who asks to remain anonymous. Nevertheless, we will name the official who gave us the leaked budget memo. Although he asked for anonymity, he has since publicly accused our reporter of fabricating the memo, and revealing that he supplied it is the only way to show that she did not.
questions.stem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the editor's reasoning?
choices: Anyone who has been promised confidentiality forfeits that promise by knowingly supplying false information to the party who made it.
A commitment made to one person should be broken only if breaking it is the sole means of preventing an unjust harm to someone else.
When honoring a commitment to one person would leave another person unjustly harmed, one should seek a remedy for the harm that leaves the commitment intact.
No one should be promised confidentiality whose conduct is a matter of legitimate public concern, as a public official's conduct is.
A promise to shield someone may be broken if that person uses it as cover to wrong another and breaking it is the only remedy.
questions.explanation: The editor overrides an ordinary promise because the official, hidden by his anonymity, falsely accused the reporter, and naming him is the only way to clear her. (E) states that exception abstractly: the protected person used the shield as cover to wrong another, and breaking the promise is the only remedy. (B) gives only a necessary condition, so it can't license naming him; (C) says to find a remedy that keeps the promise; (A)'s condition isn't met, since the memo was genuine; (D) is about making promises, not keeping them.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The newspaper will name the official despite his request for anonymity.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The paper ordinarily keeps such promises; the official publicly accused the reporter of fabricating the memo he supplied; naming him is the only way to show she didn't.

breakdown.analysis: The editor concedes the general rule (keep the promise) and claims an exception. What triggers it? Two things together: the official used his hidden role to attack the reporter falsely, and naming him is the only way to clear her. A principle-justify answer has to tell you to do what the conclusion says, triggered by these facts. Expect the right answer to be abstract: translate 'promise to shield,' 'uses it as cover,' 'wrong another' back into the story. Watch for a principle that states only a necessary condition, one whose condition isn't met, and one that reaches the opposite verdict.

choices.note: Tempting, because it lets a confidentiality promise lapse and sounds like the story. But its condition isn't met: the official gave the paper a genuine memo. His false statement was made to the public, about the reporter.

Tempting: it mentions the 'sole means' and an unjust harm, which fit the facts. But 'only if' makes those a necessary condition for breaking the promise, not a sufficient one. It tells you when you may not break a commitment, never when you should. A principle-justify answer has to tell you to do what the conclusion says.

This reaches the opposite verdict. It says to fix the harm without breaking the commitment, and the stimulus says naming the official is the only way to clear the reporter. It doesn't support naming him.
About whether to make such promises in the first place, not whether to keep one already made. Wrong question.

CORRECT. The promise to shield is the paper's pledge of anonymity; the person shielded is the official; hidden behind it, he wronged the reporter by falsely accusing her of fabrication; naming him is the only remedy. Every condition is met, and 'may be broken' licenses naming him.

questions.stimulus: Economist: Some fear that the new tax on sugary drinks will hurt small grocers. Admittedly, sales of sugary drinks at small grocers have fallen since the tax took effect. But shoppers who stop buying sugary drinks generally buy other beverages instead, so the amount they spend at small grocers is unlikely to fall much. Hence, the tax is unlikely to hurt small grocers significantly.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the economist's argument?
choices: Shoppers who stop buying sugary drinks at small grocers generally continue to buy their other groceries at those same stores.
Since the tax took effect, sales of sugary drinks have fallen even more sharply at supermarkets than at small grocers.
Small grocers in the region have faced growing competition from online retailers over the past several years.
Some shoppers who stopped buying sugary drinks have switched to beverages that cost them more than the sugary drinks did.
Small grocers earn far more profit on each sugary drink they sell than on the beverages shoppers switch to instead.
questions.explanation: The economist moves from 'shoppers will spend about as much' to 'grocers won't be hurt.' (E) breaks that step: if the replacement beverages earn far less profit, the same spending leaves grocers worse off. (C) is the trap: it shows small grocers are struggling, but not because of the tax. (A) and (D) support the economist.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The sugary-drink tax is unlikely to hurt small grocers significantly.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Concession: sugary-drink sales at small grocers have fallen. But shoppers switch to other beverages (intermediate conclusion: their spending at small grocers won't fall much).

breakdown.analysis: Look at the last step. Spending at the store holds steady, so the store isn't hurt? Not if a dollar of soda earns the grocer more than a dollar of juice. Revenue isn't profit. The concession is granted and the switching claim may be true; the weak spot is the jump from shoppers' spending to the grocers' well-being. We need an answer that shows steady spending can still mean lost profit.

choices.note: This strengthens. If shoppers keep buying their other groceries there, the store keeps their business.
Supermarkets aren't the issue. A bigger drop elsewhere doesn't show small grocers are hurt.
Tempting, because it shows small grocers are struggling. But the argument is about the tax's effect. Pressure from online retailers is true and unrelated.
This strengthens. If shoppers switch to pricier drinks, spending at the grocer may even rise.

CORRECT. Grant everything the economist says about spending. If the grocer makes much more on each sugary drink than on its replacements, the same spending brings in less profit, and the tax can hurt small grocers after all.

questions.stimulus: Any city whose transit system runs trains at least every ten minutes during rush hour will see its rush-hour train ridership rise from year to year. Rush-hour train ridership in Brennock has been rising steadily in each of the past five years. So Brennock's transit system must be running its trains at least every ten minutes during rush hour.
questions.stem: Which one of the following arguments exhibits a flawed pattern of reasoning most similar to that exhibited by the argument above?
choices: Only a vineyard that harvests all of its grapes by hand can qualify for the regional quality seal. The Ostrander vineyard's wines carry that seal this year. So the Ostrander vineyard must be harvesting all of its grapes by hand.

Any choir that rehearses each new piece at least six times will perform it without major errors. The Linden Choir rehearsed its newest piece only four times. So the Linden Choir will make major errors when it performs that piece.

Every hospital in the region that adopted electronic charts last year reduced its paperwork costs. So electronic charts will reduce paperwork costs at any hospital in the region that adopts them at some point in the future.

Most candidates endorsed by the Courier newspaper win their elections. Pelham has been endorsed by the Courier this year. So Pelham will certainly win the election that she is now contesting against two rivals.

Hollis Bistro's chef must have trained at the Lyon Institute. After all, the bistro has earned a top rating from critics this year, and no restaurant whose chef trained at that institute has ever failed to earn one.
questions.explanation: The original affirms the consequent: frequent trains → rising ridership; ridership is rising; so frequent trains. (E) does the same with the conclusion first and the rule phrased as 'no restaurant ... has failed to earn one': trained at Lyon → top rating; top rating; so trained at Lyon. (A) looks identical but is valid, because 'only' makes the seal require hand-harvesting. (B) commits a different conditional error (denying the antecedent).

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Brennock's transit system must run trains at least every ten minutes at rush hour.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Trains every ten minutes → rising rush-hour ridership; Brennock's rush-hour ridership is rising.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: If X, then Y. Y. So X. (Affirming the consequent: treats a sufficient condition as necessary.)

breakdown.analysis: Diagram the original: frequent trains → rising ridership. We see rising ridership and conclude frequent trains. That's the reversal: the rule never says frequent trains are the only way to get rising ridership. We need an answer with the same mistake: a rule 'if X then Y,' a case that has Y, and a conclusion that it has X. Watch two traps: one that looks the same but uses 'only' (which makes it valid), and one that makes the other famous conditional mistake.

choices.note: The near-miss. It looks just like the original, but 'only a vineyard that harvests by hand can qualify' means seal → hand-harvested. Ostrander has the seal, so hand-harvesting follows. That's valid. The original's rule runs the other way.

Flawed, but differently. Rule: six rehearsals → no major errors. The choir had fewer than six, so the argument concludes errors. That's denying the antecedent, not affirming the consequent. Same family, different mistake.
A generalization from past adopters to all future adopters. No conditional is reversed. Different flaw.
Turns 'most' into 'certainly.' That's a probability-to-certainty flaw, not a reversed conditional.

CORRECT. Rearranged: trained at Lyon → top rating ('no such restaurant has failed to earn one'). Hollis has a top rating, so the argument concludes its chef trained at Lyon. Same reversal as the original, just with the conclusion stated first.

questions.stimulus: Last season, a certain theater began selling any seats still unsold on the day of a performance at half the regular price. The theater sells no other discounted tickets, and its regular price has not changed. Compared with the season before, the theater sold 4 percent fewer regular-price tickets last season, yet its total revenue from ticket sales was exactly the same.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the information above?
choices: Some patrons who had bought regular-price tickets in advance in earlier seasons waited last season to buy half-price tickets instead.
Most of the people who bought half-price tickets last season had never before attended a performance at the theater.
Most of the seats that went unsold in the season before were filled last season by buyers of half-price tickets.
Last season the theater sold a larger number of tickets than the season before, while its revenue per ticket fell.
On average, the theater's performances were closer to selling out last season than they had been the season before.
questions.explanation: Revenue held steady while regular-price sales fell 4 percent, so half-price sales exactly replaced the lost revenue; each half-price ticket earns half as much, so the theater sold twice as many half-price tickets as the regular tickets it lost. Total tickets therefore rose, and with the same revenue spread over more tickets the average price fell (D). (A) is the trap: the cannibalization story is natural, but nothing shows why regular sales dropped or that any patron switched. (C) confuses fewer regular tickets with fewer tickets overall, and (E) is contradicted by the flat revenue.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1. Last season, unsold seats were sold on performance day at half price; 2. no other discounts, and the regular price didn't change; 3. regular-price tickets sold fell 4 percent from the season before; 4. total ticket revenue was exactly the same.

breakdown.analysis: Hard to prephrase without the math, so do it. Say the season before, the theater sold 100 tickets at $10: $1,000, all full price. Last season: 96 regular tickets = $960, so half-price tickets brought in $40, at $5 each = 8 tickets. Total: 104 tickets, and $1,000 / 104 ≈ $9.62 per ticket. More tickets, lower average price, and that holds for any starting numbers. Most students pick (A) because the story writes itself: regulars waited for the bargain. But the stimulus never says why regular sales fell 4 percent; maybe a few subscribers moved away. A plausible story isn't a supported one. Also watch (E): more tickets doesn't mean fuller houses unless the number of performances held steady, and we aren't told that.

choices.note: Tempting. It's the obvious explanation for the 4 percent drop. But the facts don't say why regular sales fell, and the numbers work just as well if not a single patron switched. Possible isn't supported.
We know nothing about who bought the half-price tickets. New information.

Tempting, since half-price sales did rise. But we don't know how many seats went unsold before, so we can't say most were filled. We know only that half-price sales were about twice the lost regular sales.

CORRECT. Same revenue, 4 percent fewer full-price tickets, so the gap was filled by half-price tickets at twice the count: total tickets rose. The same money spread over more tickets means a lower average price.
Tempting, because more tickets were sold. But we don't know whether the number of performances stayed the same; with more performances, each could be emptier. Not supported.

questions.stimulus: When the leaves of a tomato plant wilt in summer, the cause is usually either a lack of water or a fungus attacking the roots. The tomato plants in Ines's garden wilted last week, even though it rained heavily every day that week. So the wilting was probably caused by a root fungus.
questions.stem: The pattern of reasoning in which one of the following arguments is most similar to that in the argument above?
choices: Drops in a museum's ticket sales are usually caused either by bad weather or by blocked access to the museum. The museum's sales fell last month, and the main road leading to it was closed for repairs all month. So the drop was probably caused by blocked access.

Damage like that on the apples in this orchard is usually caused either by hail or by insects. The apples were damaged this summer, even though the orchard was sprayed against insects all season. So the damage must have been caused by hail.

The bakery's sourdough probably failed to rise this morning because its starter has grown weak. Bread like this usually fails to rise either because the kitchen is too cold or because the starter is weak, and the kitchen has been unusually warm all week.

The engine in Kwame's car probably overheated because of a coolant leak. An engine of the same model overheated last summer in his neighbor's car, and that time the cause turned out to be a leak in the coolant line.

Crop failures in this valley are usually caused either by drought or by an early frost. This year the valley has had plenty of rain and the frost has come late. So this year's crops in the valley will probably not fail.
questions.explanation: The original names the two usual causes of an effect, rules one out for this case, and concludes the other is probably responsible. (C) does the same with the conclusion stated first. (B) matches the structure but concludes 'must' from 'usually'; (A) confirms one cause instead of ruling out the other; (E) rules out both causes to predict that the effect won't happen.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The wilting was probably caused by a root fungus.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Wilting is usually caused by lack of water or root fungus; it rained heavily all week.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: Effect E usually has cause A or cause B. E happened, and A is ruled out. So B probably caused it.

breakdown.analysis: No conditionals to diagram here. Find the skeleton: two usual causes, one eliminated, the other probably the culprit. Note the strength words: 'usually' in the premise, 'probably' in the conclusion. The right answer must keep both. Watch for a choice that matches everything but turns 'probably' into 'must,' and for one that rules out both causes.

choices.note: Tempting: two usual causes, then a conclusion about one. But it reaches the conclusion by finding evidence for blocked access, not by ruling out bad weather. Different method.
The structure matches, but the strength doesn't. From 'usually caused by' you can conclude 'probably,' not 'must.' One element is off, and that's enough.
CORRECT. Two usual causes (cold kitchen, weak starter); one ruled out (the kitchen is warm); so probably the other. The conclusion just comes first.
An analogy with one earlier case, not an elimination between two usual causes. Different reasoning.
It rules out both usual causes and predicts the effect won't happen. The original rules out one cause of an effect that did happen.

questions.stimulus: A publisher claims that a novelist's latest book has already become her most widely read. But a survey shows that most people who have read any of the novelist's earlier books have not read the new one. So the publisher's claim must be false.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the argument is flawed in that the argument
choices: confuses the number of people who have read a book with the number of copies of that book that the publisher has sold to bookstores and libraries
overlooks the possibility that some people who have read the novelist's earlier books have also read the new one
treats evidence about the readers of all her earlier books taken together as though it showed how the new book compares with each of them
