fails to consider that most readers of the earlier books may intend to read the novelist's new book eventually
treats a claim about how widely a book has been read as though it were a claim about how highly it is regarded
questions.explanation: The publisher's claim compares the new book with each earlier book, but the survey pools everyone who read any earlier book. A book can miss most of that combined group and still beat every single earlier book: if three earlier books each had 100 different readers, the new book could reach 120 of those 300 people and top them all (C). (B) is the trap: 'most have not read it' already allows that some have, so the argument doesn't overlook it.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The publisher's claim that the new book is the novelist's most widely read is false.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Most people who have read any of her earlier books (taken as one group) have not read the new one.

breakdown.analysis: Most widely read compared with what? With each earlier book, one at a time. But the survey lumps together everyone who read any earlier book. Picture it: three earlier books, each with 100 different readers, so 300 earlier readers. The new book is read by 120 of them. Most earlier readers (180 of 300) skipped it, yet 120 beats every single earlier book's 100. That's a whole-vs.-each (group-vs.-member) slip, and it's worth knowing. New readers who never read her before only widen the gap. We need an answer that says the argument uses a fact about the pooled group to judge a book-by-book comparison.

choices.note: The argument talks about readers throughout, never sales or copies. A real-sounding confusion the argument doesn't make.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: The book sold 50,000 copies, so 50,000 people have read it.

choices.note: Tempting, because it borrows the survey's own terms. But 'most have not read it' already allows that some have. The argument doesn't overlook this, and it wouldn't save the publisher's claim anyway.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Most of last year's members didn't renew, so no one from last year renewed.

choices.note: CORRECT. The claim is book against book; the evidence is about the combined audience of all the earlier books. Missing most of that combined audience is compatible with having more readers than any one earlier book.
Future plans don't matter. The publisher says the book has already become her most widely read.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Few people have read the book yet, so it will never be popular.

choices.note: Neither the publisher nor the argument says anything about how good the book is.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Her latest book has the most readers, so it must be her best.

passages.title: Brod’s edition of The Trial
passages.subject: humanities
passages.text:
When Franz Kafka died in 1924, he left instructions that his friend Max Brod burn his unpublished manuscripts. Brod instead published them, beginning in 1925 with The Trial, a novel Kafka had abandoned a decade earlier. Brod’s edition gave readers what Kafka never produced: a single continuous text, its chapters set in an order Brod chose, its incomplete chapters set aside, and its spelling and punctuation brought into line with standard usage. Such constructed editions have drawn sharp criticism from textual scholars, who argue that they misrepresent the works they claim to rescue and that a responsible edition would present the manuscripts as they stand.

The Trial is the critics’ favorite example. Kafka left the novel as separate bundles of pages, each headed with a chapter title, none numbered, several unfinished. Yet the 1925 edition settles the novel’s order in Kafka’s name, with little in the text itself to mark where Brod’s judgments begin. Readers have long admired the novel’s steady progress from Josef K.’s arrest to his execution as deliberate design, though Kafka apparently wrote the closing chapter at nearly the same time as the opening one and never fixed the sequence of what lies between. And because translators worked from Brod’s text, his arrangement came to seem simply the novel itself. An editor’s provisional judgment, the critics conclude, hardened into a permanent text.

These objections are serious, but they tell against careless constructed editions rather than against the practice itself. Even a novel its author saw through the press reflects choices made by others: editors who proposed cuts, copy editors who regularized punctuation, typesetters whose errors went uncorrected. No one concludes that such novels are not really their authors’ work. A constructed edition differs from them in degree, not in kind. What matters is not whether an editor intervenes but whether the intervention is disclosed.

Nor need a constructed edition conceal anything. The critical edition published in 1990 also offers a continuous reading text, but it sets the unfinished chapters apart, and a companion volume explains how the chapter order was reached and records the manuscript’s cancellations and variants. Readers who wish to know where the author ends and the editor begins can find out; readers who wish simply to read the novel can do that too. The alternative the critics favor has been tried: a 1997 facsimile edition issued each bundle as a separate booklet, leaving readers to choose the order. Such editions have real value, but almost no one except specialists reads them, and a novel that survives only in that form survives, for most readers, in name alone. A candid reading text, by contrast, can serve both the reader who wants the novel and the reader who wants to know how it was made.

passages.title: Adverse possession and the industry rationale
passages.subject: law
passages.text:
Passage A

In most common-law jurisdictions, a person who occupies another’s land openly and without permission for an unbroken period fixed by statute, commonly ten to twenty years, acquires title to it, and the record owner’s claim is extinguished. The doctrine of adverse possession is often described as a concession to wrongdoers, an awkward exception to the principle that no one should profit from a trespass. That description misunderstands it.

Land is scarce, and land left idle benefits no one. The doctrine transfers title from owners who leave land unused to possessors who fence it, graze it, plant it, or build on it. The statutory period is best understood not as a measure of the owner’s patience but as a measure of the possessor’s investment. A possessor who has worked land for that long has typically sunk labor and money into it that ejection would destroy, while an owner who has ignored the land for as long has shown how little it means to him.

This account explains a feature of the doctrine that otherwise looks puzzling: under the prevailing American rule, it does not matter whether the possessor believed the land was hers or knew that it was not. If the doctrine existed to protect honest mistakes, her state of mind would be decisive. Because it exists to reward productive use, her state of mind is beside the point; a knowing possessor who farms a neglected field contributes as much as a mistaken one.

So understood, the doctrine needs no apology. It is the law’s means of ensuring that land does not lie fallow merely because the person holding title has lost interest in it.

Passage B

Defenders of adverse possession often present it as a reward for industry, moving land from idle owners to productive possessors. Court decisions fit this account poorly. Courts have awarded title to possessors who did little more than fence a pasture and graze a few animals. Yet in 1937 the Supreme Court of Indiana denied title to a company that had for decades shown paying visitors through a cave, part of which lay beneath a neighbor’s land, because the neighbor had no way of knowing the cave extended beneath his property. Visibility, not productivity, decided the case, as it often does.

The industry account also equates an owner’s nonuse with neglect. But some owners leave land unused deliberately, to let a woodland regenerate or to protect a watershed. Such restraint is an exercise of ownership, not a sign of indifference to it.

Most tellingly, many statutes lengthen the period when the owner is a minor or legally incapacitated as the possession begins, so that a possessor’s labor in those years does nothing to hasten her title. Such rules make sense only if the doctrine is concerned with an owner’s failure to object to a possession that the owner could have noticed and challenged. A rule designed to reward labor would have no reason to discount labor performed while the owner happened to be a child.

passages.title: Mobile telephones and Kerala’s fish markets
passages.subject: social-science
passages.text:
Economists hold that when goods can move freely between markets, the price of a good should differ between those markets by no more than the cost of moving it, since any larger gap would invite traders to buy where the good is cheap and sell where it is dear. Yet in many poor regions, prices for the same good vary widely among markets only a few miles apart. One common explanation is that transport there is too slow or too costly; another is that sellers do not learn what prices prevail elsewhere until it is too late to act.

The economist Robert Jensen’s study of the sardine fishery off Kerala, in southern India, offers an unusually clean test of the second explanation. In the late 1990s, fishermen there typically sold their catch at the beach nearest their village. Because fish spoil quickly and a boat could seldom try more than one market in a trip, a fisherman landing at a glutted beach had little choice but to accept whatever he was offered, and on some days catches went unsold and were dumped while buyers at a market a few miles along the coast went without. Between 1997 and 2000, mobile telephone service reached the coast, and fishermen began calling buyers from sea to learn where prices were highest before choosing where to land.

What makes the study persuasive is the sequence in which service arrived. Coverage reached the three districts Jensen surveyed in different years, and in each the spread of prices across its markets fell sharply, and the dumping of unsold fish all but ceased, once its own fishermen gained service: not before, and not when a neighboring district did. Improvements in boats, roads, or demand that affected the whole coast at once could not produce that staggered pattern. Nor were the gains confined to fishermen who owned telephones: once some boats began steering away from glutted markets, those markets were less glutted for everyone who landed there. Fishermen’s profits rose, and the prices consumers paid fell slightly, since fish that would once have been wasted now reached buyers.

The study is often cited as proof that spreading information technology will by itself integrate the markets of poor regions, but that reading asks more of it than it can bear. Kerala’s fishermen were unusually well placed to act on what they learned: markets lay close together along the coast, and a boat already at sea could make for any of several at little added cost. Where markets lie days apart, or where sellers lack the means to store or carry their goods, a price report may arrive in good time and still change nothing. Information, in other words, narrows price gaps only where sellers are already able to act on it.

passages.title: Varve dating and its central assumption
passages.subject: natural-science
passages.text:
In many lakes fed by glacial meltwater, sediment accumulates in annual bands called varves, a term introduced by the Swedish geologist Gerard De Geer, who used them to date the retreat of the last ice sheet across Sweden. Each summer, meltwater carries silt and sand into the lake, where coarse particles settle quickly into a thick layer; in winter, when ice seals the lake and inflow nearly stops, the finest clay settles into a thin layer above it. Because each coarse-and-fine pair, or couplet, ordinarily represents one year, sediment at any depth can be dated by counting the couplets above it.

The method thus assumes something about the lake itself: that its inflow rises to a single peak and falls to a single lull each year. What a couplet records is not a year as such but one surge of inflow followed by slack water. A lake that receives two distinct floods a year, separated by a pause long enough for fine particles to settle, can lay down two couplets in that year. For this reason, varve counts are often checked against independent markers, such as calibrated radiocarbon dates from buried land plants, or layers of volcanic ash matched chemically to eruptions of known date.

A simplified, hypothetical study shows how such checks work. A small alpine lake lies just below a cirque glacier at the head of its valley, a kind of glacier that has advanced and retreated repeatedly in recent millennia. Its cores held about 4,100 couplets above the gravel the glacier left when it last withdrew from the basin, yet leaves from the lowest sediment gave a calibrated radiocarbon date of only about 2,050 years. The investigators considered radiocarbon error but set it aside: the most common source of such error in lake sediment, carbon from ancient limestone dissolved in the water, makes samples appear older than they are, not younger, and does not affect leaves, which take their carbon from the air. They concluded instead that the count was accurate but had been misread. The lake, they proposed, receives one flood in late spring, when snow melts on the low slopes around it, and another in late summer, when the glacier at the head of the valley reaches its peak melt, with weeks of slack inflow between.

Other findings fit the proposal. A band of ash in the cores, from an eruption that historical records place about 1,140 years before the cores were taken, lies beneath roughly 2,280 couplets, and the couplets below it number close to twice the remaining 910 years. So do the coarse layers: the low slopes are dark slate and the valley head pale, feldspar-rich granite, and slate-rich layers alternate regularly with granite-rich ones. In a neighboring valley that holds no glacier, a lake’s couplet count and radiocarbon age agree within a few decades. A handful of intervals in the cores hold single rather than double couplets; the investigators attribute these to cool summers in which the glacier sent no flood.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?
choices: Constructed editions such as Brod’s edition of The Trial take no greater liberties with an author’s work than ordinary publishing does, so textual scholars’ objections to them are unfounded.
The critics’ objections to constructed editions are best answered not by abandoning such editions but by preparing them in a way that makes the editor’s interventions plain.
Brod’s edition of The Trial illustrates how an editor’s provisional arrangement of an unfinished novel can harden into the text that readers take to be the author’s own.
Editions that reproduce an unfinished novel’s manuscripts as they stand serve only specialists and should therefore give way to constructed editions meant for general readers.
Because constructed editions present an editor’s decisions as the author’s own, editors of unfinished novels should present the surviving manuscripts as they stand.
questions.explanation: The author concedes that the critics’ objections are serious but says they tell against careless constructed editions, and that what matters is “whether the intervention is disclosed,” as the 1990 edition shows it can be. B says this in other words. A drops the author’s “careless” qualifier and contradicts “in degree, not in kind,” C is the critics’ argument from the second paragraph, D overstates the author’s concession that facsimile editions have real value, and E is the critics’ conclusion.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the author’s overall position, not the critics’ and not a supporting detail.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 1 (the critics’ position), paragraph 3 (the author’s turn and test), paragraph 4 (a disclosed edition and the facsimile alternative).

breakdown.analysis: Who is talking where? Paragraphs 1–2 are the critics. Paragraph 3 starts the author’s reply: the objections “tell against careless constructed editions rather than against the practice itself.” Paragraph 4: a reading edition can disclose everything, and facsimiles go unread. So the main point is: keep constructed editions, but disclose the editor’s work. Watch for two traps: the critics’ view dressed up as the main point (C, E), and the author’s view pushed too far (A, D).

choices.note: Tempting, because the author does compare constructed editions to ordinary publishing. But the author says they differ “in degree, not in kind,” which means they take more liberties, not the same. And the author calls the objections “serious,” not unfounded. Too strong.

CORRECT. The objections are answered by disclosure (“what matters is … whether the intervention is disclosed”), and the author’s answer is to make such editions with disclosure rather than stop making them.
This is the critics’ case from paragraph 2. The author grants it is serious but uses it to argue for a different conclusion. One paragraph’s point, and the wrong party’s.
Too strong. The author says facsimile editions “have real value.” The author wants constructed editions made well, not facsimiles abandoned.
That is the critics’ conclusion, which the author rejects.

questions.stem: The passage most strongly suggests that the chapter of The Trial in which Josef K. is executed
choices: dates from a stage at which the order of the chapters preceding it was still unsettled
was among the unfinished chapters that Brod set aside when he prepared the 1925 edition
owes its place at the end of the novel to Brod’s judgment rather than to Kafka’s
was cited by the critics as evidence that Kafka had planned the order of the middle chapters
was the last part of the novel that Kafka completed before he abandoned the manuscript
questions.explanation: The second paragraph says Kafka wrote the closing chapter at nearly the same time as the opening one and “never fixed the sequence of what lies between.” So when he wrote it, the order of the chapters before it was unsettled, and it stayed that way: A. C is the main trap: Brod settled the order of the bundles, but the passage calls the execution chapter Kafka’s “closing chapter,” so its place at the end was Kafka’s. E mistakes “closing” for “written last.”

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Infer what the passage implies, by putting two clauses together, about the execution chapter.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 2, fourth sentence; paragraph 2, third sentence (Brod settled the order).

breakdown.analysis: Two facts sit in one sentence: Kafka wrote the closing chapter early, at nearly the same time as the opening one, and he never fixed the sequence of the middle. Put them together: when the ending was written, the order of everything before it was open. The key says this without the words “opening” or “closing.” Two traps borrow other parts of the paragraph: Brod’s ordering (C) and the novel’s apparent design (D).

choices.note: CORRECT. Written near the start, with the middle’s sequence never fixed, so the order of the preceding chapters was unsettled when it was written.
Brod did set aside incomplete chapters, but nothing says this was one of them; the novel’s “progress … to his execution” shows the edition includes it.
Tempting, because Brod settled the novel’s order. But the passage calls this Kafka’s “closing chapter”: the ending was Kafka’s; what Brod decided was the middle.
Backward. The critics use its early date to show the middle’s order was never planned.
It mistakes “closing” for “written last.” The passage says it was written early, near the opening chapter.

questions.stem: The author’s attitude toward the practice of producing constructed editions of unfinished novels is most accurately described as
choices: acceptance of the practice as a regrettable necessity, since few readers will read manuscripts as they stand
approval of the practice, tempered by the reservation that an editor should not settle the order of the chapters
approval of the practice, conditioned on the editor’s making clear to readers which choices were the editor’s
enthusiasm for the practice, on the ground that all published novels reflect choices made by people other than the author
skepticism toward the practice, tempered by admiration for the candor of the 1990 critical edition
questions.explanation: The author defends constructed editions but limits the defense to editions that disclose the editor’s interventions (“What matters is not whether an editor intervenes but whether the intervention is disclosed”). That is approval conditioned on disclosure, C. B is the near miss: it qualifies the approval, but on the wrong point; the author praises the 1990 edition, which settles a chapter order and explains how it was reached.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Pick the description that names both what the author approves of and what the approval depends on.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 3 (last sentence) and paragraph 4 (the 1990 edition).

breakdown.analysis: Two choices say “approval” with a qualification, so “qualified approval” alone won’t pick the answer; you have to check what the qualification is. The author’s condition is stated outright at the end of paragraph 3: intervention is fine, concealment is not. Does the author object to an editor settling the chapter order? No: the 1990 edition settles one, explains how, and is the author’s model. We need approval conditioned on disclosure.

choices.note: Tempting, because the author admits that facsimiles reach almost no one. But the author argues for the practice as able to serve every reader, not as a necessary evil.
Tempting near miss. Right attitude, wrong qualification. The author approves of the 1990 edition, which does settle the chapter order; the condition is disclosure, not leaving the order open.
CORRECT. Approval of constructed editions, on the condition that readers can tell where the editor’s choices begin.
Too strong. The author does cite the ordinary-publishing point, but calls the critics’ objections serious and attaches a condition.
The author’s view of the practice is favorable, not skeptical; the admiration for the 1990 edition is part of that favorable view.

questions.stem: In saying that a novel surviving only in the form the critics favor would survive “in name alone” (fourth paragraph), the author most likely means that such a novel
choices: would keep its title while losing much of the text that its author actually wrote
would be credited to its author even though an editor had determined its final form
would be valued by specialists chiefly for the cancellations and variants it records
would be something most readers have heard of but have not actually read
would lose any claim to be regarded as a finished work of literature
questions.explanation: The phrase follows the claim that “almost no one except specialists reads” such editions, and it is qualified “for most readers.” So the novel would be known by name but not read: D. A is the literal trap: a facsimile loses none of the text, it reproduces all of it.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Work out what “in name alone” means in context.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4, the sentence about facsimile editions.

breakdown.analysis: Read the whole sentence: such editions have value, but almost no one except specialists reads them, so the novel survives, “for most readers, in name alone.” Survives in name = people know of it. Not in fact = they don’t read it. The trap is the literal reading: only the name (title) survives while the text is lost. But the facsimile keeps every word.

choices.note: Tempting literal reading. But a facsimile edition loses nothing; it reproduces all of Kafka’s pages. The problem is readership, not lost text.
This describes the critics’ complaint about constructed editions like Brod’s, not facsimiles.
Specialists do read such editions, but the phrase is about “most readers,” not specialists.
CORRECT. Most readers would know the novel exists but wouldn’t read it, since almost no one but specialists reads facsimiles.
The author’s point is about readership, not literary status.

questions.stem: The author would be most likely to agree with which one of the following statements about Brod’s 1925 edition of The Trial?
choices: It should be replaced by an edition that, like the 1997 facsimile, leaves readers to decide the order of the chapters for themselves.
It took no greater liberties with Kafka’s manuscripts than a publisher ordinarily takes with a novel its author has finished.
Its arrangement of the chapters is more faithful to Kafka’s intentions than the arrangement in the 1990 critical edition.
Its fault lay less in Brod’s arranging the chapters than in the text’s failure to show readers which choices were his.
Brod was justified in presenting the novel as Kafka’s alone because Kafka had given each bundle of manuscript a chapter title.
questions.explanation: The critics say Brod’s edition settles the order “with little in the text itself to mark where Brod’s judgments begin”; the author replies that the objections tell against careless editions and that “what matters is not whether an editor intervenes but whether the intervention is disclosed.” So the author locates the fault in nondisclosure, D. B is the main trap: the author says constructed editions differ from ordinary publishing “in degree,” so they take more liberties, not the same.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Infer the author’s view of Brod’s edition specifically.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 2 (what Brod’s edition did and didn’t mark), paragraph 3 (the author’s test: disclosure).

breakdown.analysis: The author never comments on Brod’s edition by name, so combine two paragraphs. The critics’ complaint about Brod: little in the text shows where his choices start. The author: intervening is fine; failing to disclose is the problem. Put together: Brod’s arranging wasn’t the sin; hiding it was. Most students who miss this pick (B), because the author does compare constructed editions to ordinary publishing. But “in degree, not in kind” means constructed editions do more, just not something different in nature.

choices.note: That is what the critics want. The author defends reading editions and says almost no one but specialists reads facsimiles.

Tempting. The author does compare constructed editions with ordinary publishing, but says they differ “in degree, not in kind,” which means they take greater liberties. The comparison shows the difference is not one of kind, not that there is no difference.
The passage never compares the two editions’ fidelity to Kafka’s intentions.
CORRECT. By the author’s own test, intervention is acceptable and nondisclosure is not, and the critics’ chief charge against Brod’s edition is that nothing in its text marks his judgments.
The passage gives no such justification, and chapter titles say nothing about order.

questions.stem: Which one of the following is most analogous to the companion volume of the 1990 critical edition of The Trial, as that volume is described in the passage?
choices: a report issued with a performing version of an unfinished symphony that sets out the grounds for the editor’s choices and lists the sketches he set aside
a recording of an unfinished symphony that includes only the passages the composer completed, omitting everything an editor would have had to supply
a performing version of an unfinished symphony, published under the composer’s name alone, in which the editor’s additions imitate the composer’s style
a facsimile of the composer’s sketches for an unfinished symphony, bound in the order in which the composer is believed to have written them
a scholar’s essay arguing that an unfinished symphony should be performed only from the composer’s sketches and never from an editor’s version
questions.explanation: The companion volume accompanies a usable reading text and discloses the editor’s work: how the chapter order was reached and what variants and cancellations the manuscript contains. A matches every element: it accompanies a performable version and explains the editor’s choices and the material left out. B and D correspond to the facsimile approach, C to Brod’s undisclosed edition, and E to the critics’ argument.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the item that plays the same role as the 1990 edition’s companion volume.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4, second and third sentences.

breakdown.analysis: What is the volume? It goes alongside a continuous reading text, and it explains the editor’s decisions and records what was set aside. Three elements: (1) a usable version exists; (2) the document accompanies it; (3) it discloses the editor’s choices and the unused material. Every wrong answer maps onto a different item in the passage: the facsimile, Brod’s edition, or the critics.

choices.note: CORRECT. A disclosure that accompanies a usable version, explaining the editor’s choices and listing what was set aside: all three elements.
This is like presenting only what the author finished, closer to the facsimile approach. There is no usable completed version and nothing explained.
This is Brod’s edition: a continuous text under the author’s name with little marking the editor’s work. The opposite of disclosure.
Tempting, since a facsimile is mentioned in the same paragraph. But this corresponds to the 1997 facsimile, not the companion volume, and it accompanies no performing version.
This corresponds to the critics’ position, not to any edition.

questions.stem: Both passages are primarily concerned with
choices: what purpose best accounts for the features of a rule letting a possessor gain title to land she does not own
whether courts have applied the doctrine of adverse possession consistently to those possessors who have substantially improved the land
whether the doctrine of adverse possession ought to be abolished as an unjustified concession to those who trespass
the special protection that statutes extend to owners who are minors or are legally incapacitated when a possession begins
the conditions under which an owner’s decision to leave his land unused should properly be regarded as a form of neglect
questions.explanation: Passage A argues that adverse possession exists to reward productive use; passage B argues that its features fit an owner’s failure to object better. Both are about the doctrine’s purpose, A. D and E are topics only passage B raises, and C is a description passage A mentions only to reject; neither passage proposes abolition.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the topic that both passages are mainly about.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage A paragraphs 2–3 (productive use); passage B first and last paragraphs (visibility, failure to object).

breakdown.analysis: A “both” answer has to fit each passage as a whole. A says the doctrine is about rewarding industry. B says it’s about the owner’s failure to object. Same question, different answers: what is the doctrine for? Eliminate anything only one passage touches.

choices.note: CORRECT. Each passage offers and defends an account of the doctrine’s purpose, using its features as evidence.
Only passage B discusses court decisions, and its point is about purpose, not consistency.
Tempting, because passage A mentions the “concession to wrongdoers” description. But A raises it only to reject it, and neither passage argues about abolition.
Only passage B mentions this, and only as evidence for its account.
Only passage B raises nonuse as deliberate restraint, in one short paragraph.

questions.stem: The author of passage A would most likely respond to passage B’s discussion of the 1937 Indiana case by
choices: conceding that the doctrine rewards an owner’s opportunity to object rather than a possessor’s productive use
arguing that the cave company’s exhibition of the cave was not a productive use of the land beneath it
maintaining that a requirement that possession be open is consistent with an aim of rewarding productive use
denying that courts in common-law jurisdictions require that a possessor’s occupation of land be open
contending that the company should have prevailed, since a possessor’s knowledge that land is another’s is irrelevant
questions.explanation: Passage A itself states the rule as requiring that the land be occupied “openly,” and it never treats that requirement as a problem for its account. So its author would most plausibly answer the cave case by saying that a doctrine aimed at rewarding productive use can still insist that the use be open, C. E is the strongest trap: it uses passage A’s own point about the possessor’s state of mind, but that point concerns belief about ownership, not concealment, and cannot override the openness requirement A accepts.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Predict passage A’s reply to passage B’s cave case.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage A paragraph 1 first sentence (“openly”) and paragraphs 2–3 (productive use; state of mind); passage B paragraph 1.

breakdown.analysis: B’s cave case: a productive, profitable use lost because it wasn’t visible. Is that fatal to A? A’s own first sentence lists “openly” as a requirement. So A already accepts that hidden use doesn’t count. A’s best reply isn’t to abandon its account or deny the facts; it’s to say a reward for productive use can come with a condition that the use be open. Most students who miss this pick (E), because A says state of mind doesn’t matter. But “state of mind” in A means belief about who owns the land; the cave case turned on whether the owner could know, which is the openness requirement.

choices.note: A says the doctrine “needs no apology” as a reward for productive use; it would not adopt B’s account.
The passage says the company showed paying visitors through the cave for decades; nothing suggests A would call that unproductive.
CORRECT. A already lists openness as a requirement, so it can treat the cave case as an application of a condition on, not a refutation of, the productive-use rationale.
Contradicts passage A’s own first sentence, which requires open occupation.

Tempting, because it reuses passage A’s state-of-mind point. But that point is about the possessor’s belief, not about whether the possession could be seen, and A accepts that possession must be open.

questions.stem: The authors of the passages would be most likely to disagree over whether
choices: the length of the statutory period is best explained by reference to what a possessor has put into the land
a possessor who knows that the land is not hers can acquire title to it under the rule that prevails in American courts
open occupation of land for the statutory period can extinguish the record owner’s claim to the land
the cave company’s use of the land beneath its neighbor’s property was a productive one
the lengthening of the period for owners who are minors when a possession begins ought to be abolished
questions.explanation: Passage A says the period is “best understood … as a measure of the possessor’s investment”; passage B argues that the rules about the period, such as its lengthening for minors, make sense only if the doctrine is about an owner’s failure to object, and that a rule designed to reward labor would not discount labor. That is a disagreement, A. In B and D only one author takes a position, C is common ground, and E is something neither proposes.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find a claim one author would affirm and the other would deny.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage A paragraph 2; passage B paragraph 3.

breakdown.analysis: For a disagree question, both authors must take a position, on opposite sides. A explicitly ties the period to the possessor’s investment. B’s last paragraph explains features of the period by the owner’s failure to object and says a labor-based rule would make no sense of them. Opposite answers to the same question. Check each wrong choice by asking: does each author actually commit on this?

choices.note: CORRECT. A says yes (“a measure of the possessor’s investment”). B says the period’s features show the doctrine is about the owner’s failure to object, not about rewarding labor.
Tempting, because passage A says this outright. But passage B never discusses the possessor’s state of mind, so we don’t know that B disagrees.
Both accept this as the basic rule; it is common ground, not disagreement.
Only passage B mentions the cave company, and A’s author says nothing about it. B itself treats the use as profitable.
Neither author proposes abolishing anything. B uses the rule as evidence.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the relationship between the two passages?
choices: Passage A describes a legal doctrine and the debate over its purpose without taking sides; passage B criticizes the doctrine on the basis of several court decisions.
Passage A defends a legal doctrine against a charge of unfairness; passage B argues that the charge is justified because of how courts apply the doctrine.
Passage A defends a legal doctrine by attributing a purpose to it; passage B argues that no purpose could justify the doctrine as courts have applied it.
Passage A proposes reforming a legal doctrine; passage B argues that the proposed reform conflicts with features of the doctrine that are well settled.
Passage A defends a legal doctrine by attributing a purpose to it; passage B argues that the doctrine’s features are better explained by a different purpose.
questions.explanation: Passage A defends adverse possession as a means of rewarding productive use. Passage B argues that the doctrine’s features (the visibility cases, the treatment of minors) fit a concern with an owner’s failure to object better. That is E. C shares E’s first half but overstates passage B, which offers its own purpose rather than claiming none could justify the doctrine; B wrongly has passage B endorsing the charge of unfairness.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Describe how passage B relates to passage A.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage A paragraphs 1 and 4; passage B first sentence and last paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: Summarize each in a phrase. A: the doctrine is justified because its purpose is rewarding productive use. B: the doctrine’s features point to a different purpose (owners’ failure to object). B doesn’t attack the doctrine; it attacks A’s explanation of it. Two choices start the same way (C and E); the second half decides it.

choices.note: Passage A takes a clear side, and passage B criticizes an account of the doctrine, not the doctrine itself.
Tempting, since passage A answers the “concession to wrongdoers” charge. But passage B never says the doctrine is unfair; it offers a different account of what the doctrine is for.
Tempting near miss: right on passage A, but passage B doesn’t say no purpose could justify the doctrine. It proposes one: concern with an owner’s failure to object.
Neither passage proposes a reform.
CORRECT. Passage A: purpose = rewarding productive use. Passage B: the features fit a different purpose better.

questions.stem: The author of passage A mentions that it does not matter whether the possessor believed the land was hers (first sentence of the third paragraph of passage A) primarily in order to
choices: point to a feature of the doctrine that favors the author’s account of its purpose over a competing account
concede a feature of the doctrine that the author’s own account of its purpose cannot readily explain
argue that courts should begin to consider whether a possessor acted in good faith before awarding title to the land
show that the doctrine was originally designed to protect possessors who made honest mistakes about ownership
rebut the charge that the doctrine rewards wrongdoers by showing that knowing possessors seldom acquire title
questions.explanation: Passage A says its account “explains a feature of the doctrine that otherwise looks puzzling,” then argues that if the doctrine protected honest mistakes, the possessor’s state of mind would matter, whereas on the productive-use account it should not. The feature thus favors the author’s account over the honest-mistake account, A. B reverses the function, and D adopts the account the author rejects.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Why does passage A bring up the irrelevance of the possessor’s state of mind?

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage A paragraph 3.

breakdown.analysis: Follow the logic. The feature: belief about ownership doesn’t matter. Rival account (protecting honest mistakes) predicts it would matter. Author’s account (rewarding use) predicts it wouldn’t. So the feature is evidence for the author over the rival. Note the key never uses the passage’s words “explains” or “puzzling”; it describes the job abstractly.

choices.note: CORRECT. The feature fits the productive-use account and would make no sense if the doctrine protected honest mistakes.
Tempting reversal: the feature “looks puzzling,” but the author says this account “explains” it. Not a concession.
The author argues the courts are right to ignore the possessor’s state of mind.
The honest-mistake account is the one the author rejects.
The passage says knowing possessors can acquire title, not that they seldom do.

questions.stem: The author of passage B would most likely respond to the claim in passage A that an owner who has ignored land for the statutory period “has shown how little it means to him” by pointing out that
choices: a possessor who has worked the land for the statutory period would lose her investment if she were ejected from it
an owner’s failure to object to an open possession, rather than his nonuse, is what shows how little the land means to him
owners who leave land unused generally do so in order to let woodland regenerate or to protect a watershed
courts rarely inquire into how much an owner values land that he has chosen to leave unused
the same outward conduct can reflect either indifference to land or a considered exercise of the rights that come with owning it
questions.explanation: Passage B says the industry account “equates an owner’s nonuse with neglect,” though some owners leave land unused deliberately, as an exercise of ownership. The point is that nonuse is ambiguous between neglect and a deliberate choice, which is E, stated abstractly. C overstates passage B’s “some owners” into “generally,” and B borrows passage B’s “failure to object” to give it a view it never expresses.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Predict how passage B’s author would answer passage A’s inference from long nonuse to indifference.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage A paragraph 2, last sentence; passage B paragraph 2 (and paragraph 3 for the trap).

breakdown.analysis: A: unused land = owner doesn’t care. B: “some owners” leave land unused on purpose, and that restraint is “an exercise of ownership.” So nonuse doesn’t tell you which you’ve got. The key never mentions woods or watersheds; it states the logic: the same behavior fits two opposite explanations. Two traps reuse B’s words: C turns “some” into “generally,” and B moves “failure to object” into a place B never puts it.

choices.note: That is passage A’s own argument about the possessor, not a reply.

Tempting. “Failure to object” is passage B’s language, but B uses it to identify the doctrine’s concern, never to say what reveals an owner’s attitude, and this concedes A’s premise that losing owners don’t care.
Tempting, because these are passage B’s examples. But B says only that “some owners” do this; “generally” is too strong, and B doesn’t need it to answer A.
Neither passage says this; B’s point is about what nonuse means, not what courts ask.
CORRECT. B’s reply is that nonuse is ambiguous: it may be neglect or a deliberate exercise of ownership, so A cannot read indifference off it.

questions.stem: Passage B raises each of the following as a difficulty for the view that adverse possession rewards industry EXCEPT:
choices: the awarding of title to occupants whose improvements to the land were minimal
the awarding of title to an occupant who knew all along that the land belonged to someone else
a decision denying title despite long and profitable use, because the owner could not have detected that use
the possibility that an owner leaves land unworked out of considered concern for its condition
a rule making the time needed to gain title depend on the owner’s circumstances rather than the occupant’s labor
questions.explanation: Passage B raises A (fence-and-graze awards), C (the cave case), D (owners who leave land unused deliberately) and E (the lengthened period when the owner is a minor or incapacitated). It never raises B: the irrelevance of a possessor’s knowledge appears only in passage A, which treats it as support for the industry view. The cave case is about the owner’s inability to know, not the possessor’s knowledge.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Four choices are difficulties passage B raises for the industry view; find the one it doesn’t raise.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: All of passage B; passage A, paragraph 3, for the source of the trap.

breakdown.analysis: Every choice is paraphrased, so match each to a sentence in passage B. Paragraph 1: slight use rewarded (A); the cave company, profitable for decades, denied title because the neighbor couldn’t know (C). Paragraph 2: owners who leave land unused on purpose (D). Paragraph 3: years that don’t count while the owner is a minor (E). That leaves B. It sounds like something a critic of adverse possession would say, and it is in the pair, but in passage A, which uses it to support the industry view. EXCEPT lesson: check which passage a point comes from, not just whether it’s in the reading.

choices.note: Raised: courts awarded title to those who did little more than fence a pasture and graze a few animals.

CORRECT. Passage B never discusses a possessor who knows the land isn’t hers. That point comes from passage A, which uses it in favor of the industry view. Don’t confuse it with the cave case, where the owner is the one who couldn’t know.
Raised: the cave company’s decades of paid exhibitions did not win it title, because the neighbor had no way of knowing.
Raised: some owners leave land unused deliberately, to let woodland regenerate or protect a watershed.
Raised: when the owner is a minor or incapacitated, the possessor’s labor in those years does nothing to hasten her title.

questions.stem: The author of passage B would be most likely to agree with which one of the following statements?
choices: As courts apply the doctrine, an owner’s failure to act against a possession counts against him only when he could have acted.
A possessor who knowingly occupies another’s land should not be permitted to acquire title to that land.
Owners who leave their land unused in order to conserve it should be exempted from the operation of the doctrine of adverse possession.
The cave company would have acquired title had it put the land beneath its neighbor’s property to more productive use.
Courts that award title to possessors whose use of the land was slight are misapplying the doctrine’s actual purpose.
questions.explanation: Passage B treats the doctrine as concerned with an owner’s failure to object “to a possession that the owner could have noticed and challenged,” and both of its examples show silence not counting against owners who could not object: the neighbor who could not know about the cave, and the owner who is a child. A generalizes that principle. C is the near miss: it borrows passage B’s conservation examples but adds an exemption passage B never proposes; B calls such restraint an exercise of ownership, not a ground for special treatment.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find a principle passage B’s author would endorse.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage B paragraph 1 (the cave case) and paragraph 3 (minors; “could have noticed and challenged”).

breakdown.analysis: B’s positive view: the doctrine punishes an owner’s failure to object, but only to a possession he “could have noticed and challenged.” Look at the two examples: the cave owner couldn’t know, and the child owner can’t act; in both, the possessor’s time doesn’t count. The principle behind both: silence counts against an owner only when he could have spoken up. That is the key, stated abstractly. The trap (C) reuses B’s woodland/watershed owners, but B never says they should be exempt. B says their restraint is a way of owning, which is a reply to A, not a proposal.

choices.note: CORRECT. This is the principle uniting the cave case and the treatment of minors: the doctrine counts an owner’s failure to object only when he could have noticed and challenged the possession.
Passage B never discusses the possessor’s state of mind, and its account (failure to object) gives no reason to bar knowing possessors.
Tempting. Passage B does defend such owners against the charge of neglect, but it proposes no exemption. Showing that nonuse can be deliberate is a reply to passage A, not a reform.
Opposite. Passage B’s point is that productivity didn’t matter; the neighbor’s inability to know decided the case.
Backward. Passage B cites these decisions as evidence of what the doctrine actually tracks (visibility), not as mistakes.

questions.stem: The primary purpose of the passage is to
choices: explain what a particular study reveals about one cause of price differences among nearby markets and caution against drawing too broad a lesson from it
argue that the spread of mobile telephones will by itself bring the prices in the markets of poor regions into line with one another
defend the economists’ principle about price gaps between markets against evidence that prices often differ widely among markets close together
describe the design of a study of Kerala’s fishery in order to show that its findings are undermined by coast-wide changes in boats, roads, and demand
compare two explanations of price differences among nearby markets and conclude that the cost of transport matters more than access to information
questions.explanation: The passage sets up two explanations of price dispersion, presents Jensen’s study as a clean test of the information explanation, explains why the study is persuasive, and then warns that it does not show information technology will integrate markets by itself. A captures both halves. B is the reading the author rejects in the last paragraph, D reverses the third paragraph, and E invents a conclusion the passage never reaches.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Name the passage’s overall job, including its last paragraph.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 1 (the puzzle and two explanations), paragraph 3 first sentence (why the study is persuasive), paragraph 4 (the caution).

breakdown.analysis: Map it: paragraph 1, a puzzle with two explanations; paragraph 2, the study; paragraph 3, why it’s convincing; paragraph 4, “that reading asks more of it than it can bear.” So: explain what the study shows, then limit it. A purpose answer that leaves out the last paragraph is half right; one that adopts the over-reading is the trap.

choices.note: CORRECT. The study shows that lack of price information was a cause of dispersion in Kerala, and the last paragraph cautions against treating that as a general law.
Tempting, because it echoes the study’s popular reputation, but this is exactly the reading the author says “asks more of it than it can bear.”
The principle is background; the passage doesn’t defend it against the evidence.
Backward. The author says those changes “could not produce that staggered pattern.”
The passage doesn’t rank the two explanations in general; in Kerala, information was what mattered.

questions.stem: The passage provides information that most helps to answer which one of the following questions?
choices: In which year did mobile telephone service first reach the fishing districts along the coast of Kerala?
By how much did the profits of Kerala’s fishermen rise after mobile telephone service arrived?
What proportion of the fishing boats in Kerala carried mobile telephones by the end of the decade?
Why did mobile telephone service reach the three districts that Jensen surveyed in different years?
Why would a fisherman landing at a glutted market usually sell there rather than try elsewhere?
questions.explanation: The second paragraph explains that because fish spoil quickly and a boat could seldom try more than one market in a trip, a fisherman landing at a glutted beach had little choice but to accept the price offered. That answers E. A is the likeliest trap: the passage gives only a range (“Between 1997 and 2000”), not the first year.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the question the passage actually answers.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 2, third sentence.

breakdown.analysis: Check each question against the text. Watch for questions the passage brushes against without answering: it gives a range of years, says profits “rose” without an amount, and says service came to districts in different years without saying why. Only E gets a real answer: spoilage plus one market per trip.

choices.note: Tempting, but the passage gives only a span (“Between 1997 and 2000”), not the year service first arrived.
The passage says profits rose, not by how much.
Never stated.
The passage says service arrived in different years but not why.
CORRECT. Fish spoil quickly and a boat could seldom try more than one market in a trip.

questions.stem: The passage most strongly suggests which one of the following about the explanation that attributes price differences among nearby markets to slow or costly transport?
choices: It is inconsistent with the principle, described in the first paragraph, that price gaps should not exceed the cost of moving goods.
It does not fit the Kerala case, where gaps narrowed when sellers’ knowledge changed, not when the means of transport did.
It was the explanation that Jensen expected his study of Kerala’s fishery to confirm before he began collecting his data.
It explains the price differences in Kerala’s markets only in the districts that were the last to gain mobile service.
It cannot explain price differences among markets in any region whose sellers have access to mobile telephones.
questions.explanation: The third paragraph rules out coast-wide changes in boats or roads, and the price gaps in each district narrowed when its fishermen gained telephone service. So in Kerala, transport was not what changed; information was. B states that implication. A misreads the first paragraph: the principle allows gaps up to the cost of transport, so a transport explanation fits it. E overgeneralizes; the last paragraph says that where transport is hard, information may change nothing.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Infer what the passage implies about the transport-cost explanation.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 1 (the two explanations), paragraph 3 (what changed and what didn’t), paragraph 4 (where transport still matters).

breakdown.analysis: The passage never evaluates the transport explanation directly, so combine. Paragraph 3: improvements in boats, roads, or demand can’t produce the staggered pattern; the gaps fell when phones came. So the narrowing in Kerala tracked information, not transport. But careful: paragraph 4 says transport can matter elsewhere. So the right answer is limited to Kerala.

choices.note: Tempting misreading. The principle says gaps shouldn’t exceed transport costs; slow or costly transport would allow larger gaps, so the explanation is consistent with the principle.
CORRECT. The narrowing came when sellers got price information, and the passage rules out changes in boats and roads as the cause.
Nothing about Jensen’s expectations.
Unsupported; the passage says gaps fell in each district once service arrived.
Too strong. Paragraph 4 says that where markets are far apart, transport limits can keep information from mattering.

questions.stem: The author discusses the order in which mobile service reached the three districts (third paragraph) primarily in order to
choices: show that mobile service spread along the Kerala coast more rapidly than roads and harbors were improved
establish that the benefits of mobile service were confined to the districts whose fishermen had gained it
explain how the timing of the changes lets the study distinguish one possible cause of them from others
illustrate how fishermen used telephone calls made while still at sea to decide at which market to land their catch
suggest that improvements in boats, roads, or demand could not have affected prices along the whole coast
questions.explanation: The paragraph opens “What makes the study persuasive is the sequence,” then says coast-wide changes could not produce a staggered pattern. The sequence lets the study tell telephone service apart from rival causes, C. B is a true-sounding consequence of the timing, but the author uses the timing to make the study persuasive, not to limit its benefits; E reuses the passage’s list of rival causes in the wrong relation, since the passage says those changes did affect the whole coast at once.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Why does the author describe the staggered arrival of service?

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 3, first three sentences.

breakdown.analysis: The paragraph tells you the job: it is what makes the study “persuasive.” Persuasive against what? Rival causes. If prices converge in each district exactly when that district gets phones, a change that hit the whole coast at once can’t explain it. That is how a natural experiment works. Two traps: B states something the timing suggests but isn’t why the author mentions it, and E garbles the rival-cause sentence.

choices.note: The passage never compares the speed of telephone service with that of roads or harbors.
Tempting, since gaps fell only once a district’s own fishermen gained service. But the author brings up the sequence to show why the study is persuasive, not to limit who benefited.
CORRECT. The staggered timing separates the arrival of service from coast-wide changes as a cause.
That is described in paragraph 2, not by the sequence of arrival.
Garbled. The passage says such improvements would affect the whole coast at once, and that is exactly why they couldn’t produce a staggered pattern.

questions.stem: The author would be most likely to agree with which one of the following statements?
choices: Wherever prices for a good differ widely among nearby markets, the main cause is that sellers lack information about prices elsewhere.
The Kerala study shows that the cost of transport has little effect on the size of the price differences among markets.
Evidence from Kerala alone cannot settle whether poor price information is what keeps prices apart among widely separated markets.
Where sellers lack the means to store or carry their goods, better price information tends to widen rather than narrow price gaps.
The staggered arrival of service in Kerala makes the study’s findings applicable to regions whose markets lie days apart.
questions.explanation: The author says Kerala’s fishermen were “unusually well placed” to act on information because their markets were close together, and warns that the study cannot bear the reading that information technology integrates markets by itself. So the author would agree that Kerala’s evidence does not decide the case of widely separated markets, C. D borrows the passage’s “store or carry” but turns “may … change nothing” into “widen,” and E misapplies the staggered timing, which shows causation in Kerala, not generality.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find a view the author would hold, drawing on the last two paragraphs.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4 (why Kerala was special; where information may not help); paragraph 3 (what the staggered timing shows).

breakdown.analysis: The author does two things with Kerala: trusts the result there (paragraph 3) and refuses to export it (paragraph 4), because Kerala’s markets were close and switching was cheap. The modest conclusion: Kerala can’t tell you what happens where markets are far apart. The key looks weak (“cannot settle”), which is why it’s hard to like. But that hedge is exactly the author’s. Traps take the author too far (A, B, D) or apply the wrong paragraph (E).

choices.note: Too broad. The author warns against generalizing from Kerala.
Tempting, because information, not transport, mattered in Kerala. But Kerala’s transport was cheap, so the study says nothing about transport costs in general; paragraph 4 suggests they can matter.
CORRECT. Kerala was “unusually well placed,” so its results don’t decide what happens where markets lie far apart.
Reuses “store or carry,” but the author says information “may … change nothing” there, not that it widens gaps.
The timing establishes the cause in Kerala; it does nothing to show the results carry over to distant markets, which the author denies.

questions.stem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the information in the passage?
choices: Fishermen who acquired mobile telephones earned more from their catches than did fishermen in the same district who had none.
The dumping of unsold fish ceased in each district some years before prices across that district’s markets converged.
Before mobile service arrived, buyers at Kerala’s beach markets typically knew more about prices elsewhere than fishermen did.
After mobile service arrived, the prices consumers paid for fish fell by a larger percentage than fishermen’s profits rose over the same period.
Before mobile service arrived, price gaps among nearby beach markets on some days exceeded the cost of moving fish between them.
questions.explanation: Before telephones, catches were dumped at a glutted market while buyers a few miles away went unserved, and the last paragraph says a boat at sea could make for any of several markets “at little added cost.” A glutted market where fish were worth nothing next to one with unmet demand is a gap far larger than that cost, so E is supported; this is exactly the kind of gap the first paragraph says traders would close if they could. A is the main trap: the passage says the gains were not confined to telephone owners and gives no comparison of their earnings.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the statement the passage supports, likely by combining paragraphs.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 1 (gaps should not exceed moving costs), paragraph 2 (dumping beside unmet demand), paragraph 4 (switching markets cost little).

breakdown.analysis: Hard to prephrase; watch for answers that add numbers or comparisons the passage never gives. Then try combining. Paragraph 2: fish dumped at one beach while buyers a few miles off went without. Paragraph 4: a boat at sea could reach several markets at little added cost. So on those days, the price difference (worthless here, wanted there) was bigger than the cost of moving the fish. That’s the “anomaly” paragraph 1 sets up: gaps larger than transport costs. Most students pick (A) because phones obviously helped their owners. But the passage says the gains spread to everyone landing at once-glutted markets, and it never compares owners with non-owners.

choices.note: Tempting, but the passage never compares owners with non-owners, and it says the gains were not confined to telephone owners. Plausible, not supported.
Contradicts paragraph 3: both changes came once the district gained service.
The passage says nothing about what buyers knew.
The passage gives no percentages, only that profits rose and prices fell “slightly.”
CORRECT. Dumping beside unmet demand a few miles away, when switching markets cost little, means the price gap exceeded the cost of moving the fish.

questions.stem: Which one of the following studies would be most useful in evaluating the claim made in the last sentence of the passage?
choices: a comparison of price differences among Kerala’s beach markets before and after mobile service reached each of Jensen’s three districts
a comparison of price differences among markets in regions that gained mobile service and in similar regions that did not during those years
a survey of how often Kerala’s fishermen called buyers at more than one market before deciding where to land their catch
a measurement of how much the cost of moving goods between markets fell in regions after mobile service arrived there
a comparison of price gaps before and after mobile service arrived along coasts with distant harbors and along coasts with nearby harbors
questions.explanation: The last sentence says information narrows price gaps only where sellers can act on it. Testing that requires cases where information improves but sellers’ ability to act differs; widely separated harbors are a case where sellers cannot readily switch markets, so E supplies the comparison. A repeats Jensen’s study, where sellers could act, and B varies information but not the ability to act, so neither can test the “only where” condition.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Pick the study that would best test the claim that information narrows price gaps only where sellers can act on it.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4, last three sentences.

breakdown.analysis: The claim has a condition: information helps only when sellers can act. To test a condition, vary it. The key does that in concrete terms: harbors days apart (can’t switch) versus close together (can switch). It never says “able to act,” so you have to connect harbor distance back to paragraph 4. B is the strong trap: it has a comparison group, but the wrong one; it tests whether information matters at all.

choices.note: This is Jensen’s study again. All three districts had sellers who could act, so it can’t test whether the effect disappears where they can’t.
Tempting, because it has a control group. But it varies information, not the ability to act, so it tests whether information matters, not whether it matters only where sellers can act.
This tells you whether Kerala’s fishermen used the information, not whether ability to act is necessary.
The claim is not about whether information lowers transport costs.
CORRECT. Same new information, different ability to act (distant versus nearby harbors), so the results would show whether the effect depends on that ability.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?
choices: The radiocarbon dates for the alpine lake’s sediment are probably mistaken, since the number of couplets in its cores indicates that the lake is about 4,100 years old.
Counting couplets dates sediment accurately only where one surge and one lull occur yearly, a condition independent markers can test, as one alpine lake shows.
The alpine lake’s cores show that couplet counts in glacier-fed lakes generally overstate the age of their sediment, so radiocarbon dating should replace counting.
Although investigators have shown that radiocarbon error cannot explain the alpine lake’s conflicting ages, they have not yet established what does explain them.
The coarse layers in the alpine lake’s cores alternate between slate-rich and granite-rich ones because two kinds of bedrock underlie the lake’s catchment.
questions.explanation: The passage explains how varve dating works, identifies the assumption it rests on (one surge and one lull a year), says counts are checked against independent markers, and then uses one alpine lake to show such checks exposing and explaining a failure of that assumption. B captures all of this. D is the near miss: the investigators did reject radiocarbon error, but the passage presents their two-floods proposal and the evidence that fits it; C turns one lake into a rule for all glacier-fed lakes.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the passage’s overall point.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 1 (the method); paragraph 2 (its assumption and the checks); paragraphs 3–4 (the alpine lake as an example).

breakdown.analysis: This passage isn’t arguing against anyone; it explains a method and then shows it at work. Paragraph 1: one couplet = one year. Paragraph 2: that holds only if the lake has one surge and one lull a year, so counts get checked. Paragraphs 3–4: one lake where the check caught a doubling and the investigators found why. So the main point has to cover the method’s condition and the role of checks, with the lake as an illustration. The wrong answers each grab one piece of the lake case.

choices.note: This is the possibility the investigators set aside: the passage keeps the radiocarbon age and reinterprets the couplets.
CORRECT. The method’s condition (paragraph 2), the checks that test it, and the alpine lake as the example (paragraphs 3–4).
Tempting, because the lake’s count does overstate its age. But that’s one lake, the method normally works, and the passage never suggests abandoning it.
Tempting near miss. The investigators did set radiocarbon error aside, but they then proposed two floods a year, and paragraph 4 gives findings that fit. The explanation isn’t missing.
One finding from paragraph 4, not the main point.

questions.stem: In concluding that the couplet count “was accurate but had been misread” (third paragraph), the investigators most likely mean that
choices: some couplets were overlooked because they were too thin to be distinguished from those above and below them
the radiocarbon ages have been taken to date the lake as a whole when they date only the leaf fragments
the couplets in the cores were formed by some process other than the melting of snow and glacial ice
the cores record the number of depositional cycles accurately but not the number of years that elapsed
the count is accurate, but the couplets record the retreat of the glacier rather than the age of the lake
questions.explanation: The investigators accept that there are about 4,100 couplets but deny that each represents a year: two floods each year leave two couplets. D puts that abstractly. C is the near miss: the proposal changes how many couplets form each year, not what process forms them; both floods are meltwater, from snow and from the glacier.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Interpret the investigators’ phrase.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 2 (what a couplet records); paragraph 3, last two sentences.

breakdown.analysis: The “count” is the number of couplets. The “misreading” is the rule that one couplet = one year. The investigators keep the number and change the rule: two couplets a year. Paragraph 2 already told you what a couplet really records: one surge followed by slack water, not a year as such. The key says this in its own words.

choices.note: That would make the count wrong, which the investigators deny.
The investigators keep the radiocarbon age; they don’t reinterpret it.
Tempting, but both floods are meltwater (snow in spring, glacier in summer). What changes is the number per year, not the process.
CORRECT. The number of couplets (depositional cycles) is right; the assumption that each is a year is wrong.
The couplets lie above the gravel left by the retreat, so they record time since then; the investigators don’t say otherwise.

questions.stem: It can be inferred from the passage’s remarks about the most common source of radiocarbon error in lake sediment that, had such error affected the samples from the lake,
choices: the samples would have appeared younger than they actually are, which would explain the discrepancy
the leaf fragments would have been affected more strongly than other material in the lake’s sediment
the lake’s true age would differ even more from the age the couplets indicate
it would also account for the intervals in the cores that contain single rather than double couplets
it would have been detected because no limestone lies within the area that drains into the lake
questions.explanation: The passage says the common error makes samples appear older than they are. If the 2,050-year radiocarbon date were inflated by it, the lake would be even younger than 2,050 years, and the conflict with the 4,100 couplets would grow. That is C. A reverses the direction of the error, which is exactly why the investigators set it aside.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Work out what follows from the passage’s point about the common radiocarbon error.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 3, second and third sentences (the two ages; the common error).

breakdown.analysis: Couplets say 4,100 years; radiocarbon says 2,050. To rescue the couplets, you’d need radiocarbon to be making the lake look too young. But the common error makes samples look older. So if it were at work, the true age would be under 2,050, even further from 4,100. Most students who miss this pick (A), assuming the error goes the convenient way. The passage’s whole point is that it goes the other way.

choices.note: Reversed. The passage says the error makes samples appear older, not younger, which is why it can’t explain the gap.
Reversed: leaves take their carbon from the air, so the error doesn’t affect them.
CORRECT. An inflated radiocarbon date means the lake is even younger than 2,050 years, widening the gap with the couplet count.
Nothing connects the radiocarbon error to the single-couplet intervals.
The passage names slate and granite in the catchment but never says limestone is absent, and the investigators don’t argue this.

questions.stem: The author mentions the lake in a neighboring valley that holds no glacier (fourth paragraph) primarily in order to
choices: show that counting couplets yields accurate dates only for lakes that lie in valleys holding no glacier
explain why the ash from the eruption does not appear in the sediment of the neighboring valley’s lake
suggest that couplets whose coarse layers are mostly slate form only in lakes that are not fed by glaciers
offer a case lacking the factor to which the investigators attribute the anomaly, in which the anomaly does not occur
account for the handful of intervals in the cores that contain single rather than double couplets
questions.explanation: The investigators attribute the doubled couplets to the glacier’s separate late-summer flood. The neighboring lake has no glacier, and there couplets and radiocarbon agree, as the proposal predicts. D describes this control case abstractly. A is the main trap: it overgeneralizes one comparison into a rule about all glacier-fed lakes, though the passage says couplets ordinarily represent one year in such lakes.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Why does the author bring up the neighboring lake?

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4, third sentence; paragraph 3 (the glacier’s role).

breakdown.analysis: The proposed cause: the glacier’s second flood. Neighboring lake: no glacier, and the couplets match the radiocarbon age. That’s a control: remove the proposed cause, the effect goes away. The right answer will describe that role without naming the glacier. The trap (A) turns one comparison into a sweeping rule.

choices.note: Tempting, but too strong. The first paragraph says couplets normally represent one year in glacier-fed lakes; the problem at this lake is a second flood each year, not glaciers as such.
The passage never says the ash is absent from the neighboring lake.
Nothing suggests slate couplets form only in glacier-free lakes; at the alpine lake they form every spring.
CORRECT. No glacier, no second flood, no doubling: a comparison case that supports the investigators’ explanation.
The last sentence handles those intervals, with the cool-summer explanation; the neighboring lake has nothing to do with them.

questions.stem: On the basis of the passage, in which one of the following lakes would counting couplets be most likely to overstate the age of the sediment?
choices: a lake fed by two glaciers on different kinds of bedrock, both of which reach their peak melt during the same few weeks of summer
a lake fed by a glacier that has grown over the centuries, so that its summer floods now carry far more sediment than they once did
a lake without a glacier whose single stream floods with spring snowmelt and again, after a dry summer, with heavy autumn rains
a lake in which snowmelt from the surrounding slopes is followed, with no pause, by the peak melt of a glacier at the valley’s head
a lake whose catchment contains ancient limestone, so that carbon dissolved from the rock enters the lake’s water each year
questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says what a couplet really records: one surge of inflow followed by slack water long enough for fine particles to settle. C has two surges a year (spring melt, autumn rain) separated by a dry summer, plus the winter lull, so it would lay down two couplets a year and a count would double the sediment’s age. A and D copy features of the alpine lake (two sources, a glacier at the valley head) but give only one surge a year; the no-glacier lake in paragraph 4 makes C look safe, but the glacier was never the point.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Apply the passage’s account of how couplets form to new lakes; find the one that would give more than one couplet a year.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 2 (a couplet = one surge followed by slack water); paragraph 3 (the alpine lake’s two floods with weeks of slack between).

breakdown.analysis: So what made the alpine lake’s count go wrong: the glacier, the two kinds of rock, or something else? Paragraph 2 answers it: two distinct floods a year with a pause between them. That is the only condition that matters. Check each lake for it: 1. Two surges a year? 2. A slack interval between them? The traps copy surface features of the alpine lake (a glacier, two bedrocks, snowmelt plus glacial melt) without both conditions, and the right answer has no glacier at all, which the neighboring-valley lake in paragraph 4 tempts you to read as a guarantee of accuracy.

choices.note: Tempting near miss. Two sources on two rocks, like the alpine lake, but they peak in the same weeks, so the lake gets one surge a year and one couplet.
More sediment makes thicker layers, not more of them. Still one summer surge a year.

CORRECT. Spring flood, dry summer (slack), autumn flood, winter (slack): two surge-and-slack cycles a year, so two couplets a year, and a count would overstate the age by about double. No glacier is needed; the glacier only mattered at the alpine lake because it supplied the second flood.
Tempting near miss. Two meltwater sources, as at the alpine lake, but with no pause between them they make one continuous surge, so one couplet a year.
Limestone distorts radiocarbon ages, not couplet counts. Wrong dating method.

questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, would most call into question the investigators’ proposal about the lake?
