choices: In some lakes far from the alpine valley, couplets form more than once a year for reasons unrelated to glacial melting.
Several intervals in the cores contain only a single couplet for a year in which the proposal would lead one to expect two.
Leaf fragments that reach the floor of a lake have sometimes fallen from their trees years or even decades before they were buried.
The valley’s glacier vanished entirely about 1,500 years ago and did not re-form until roughly 700 years ago.
In late spring, meltwater from the slopes around the lake carries more sediment into it than the glacier carries in late summer.
questions.explanation: With no glacier from about 1,500 to 700 years ago, the proposal predicts single couplets for those eight centuries. That would put only about 1,840 couplets above the 1,140-year-old ash (2 × 700 + 440) and about 1,460 below it (2 × 550 + 360), not the roughly 2,280 and 1,820 found, so the counts that fit the proposal would instead count against it; D undercuts it. B is the trap: the passage already reports a handful of single-couplet intervals and the cool-summer explanation, so a few more are a loose end, not a challenge to the mechanism.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the fact that would most damage the two-floods-a-year proposal.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 3 (the glacier’s summer flood); paragraph 4 (about 2,280 couplets above the ash over 1,140 years; about twice 910 below; single-couplet intervals).

breakdown.analysis: The proposal needs a glacier sending a summer flood for the lake’s whole life, and its best evidence is that the doubling holds on both sides of the ash. D doesn’t mention couplets at all, so it looks irrelevant. Run it: no glacier from 1,500 to 700 years ago means single couplets then. Above the ash: 700 doubled years + 440 single = about 1,840, not 2,280. Below: 550 doubled + 360 single = about 1,460, not 1,820. The counts no longer fit two per year, so the proposal can’t explain its own best evidence. Most students pick (B), the anomaly the passage mentions. But the passage already accounts for it.

choices.note: Paragraph 2 already says lakes with two floods a year can do this; other lakes having other causes says nothing about whether the glacier explains this one.
Tempting. But the passage already reports single-couplet intervals, and the investigators have a cool-summer explanation; a few more are a loose end, not a refutation.
Decades-old leaves would shift the radiocarbon age by decades, nowhere near enough to close a 2,000-year gap.
CORRECT. Eight glacier-free centuries would mean eight centuries of single couplets, so the proposal would predict far fewer couplets on both sides of the ash than were found.
Which flood carries more sediment doesn’t matter; the proposal needs only that each leaves its own couplet.

questions.stimulus: Farmer: Agronomists warn that planting corn in the same field year after year steadily depletes the soil and lowers yields. But my neighbor Tolliver has planted corn in his east field every year for two decades, and last year his harvest there was one of the best in the county. So the agronomists' warning about continuous corn planting is greatly overstated.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the farmer's argument is flawed in that the argument
choices: presumes that any farming practice that does not lower crop yields must therefore improve the condition of the soil
relies on a report of a neighbor's harvest that may have been exaggerated by the neighbor himself
fails to consider whether rotating crops in the east field would cost Tolliver more than planting corn there every year
treats a single field's experience as if it settled a claim about what generally happens in such fields
overlooks the possibility that the agronomists' warning concerns some crops other than corn grown in the county
questions.explanation: The farmer rebuts a general warning about what continuous corn planting tends to do with one field that happened to do well; one exception cannot show a general tendency is overstated, which (D) names. (B) is tempting, but it only raises a possibility the argument gives no reason to suspect, and even an accurate report of one harvest would leave the flaw in place.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The agronomists' warning about planting corn year after year is greatly overstated.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Tolliver has planted corn in one field for twenty years; last year that field gave one of the county's best harvests.

breakdown.analysis: So what if one field did fine? One lucky field doesn't tell you what usually happens. Structure: 1. Experts: continuous corn tends to deplete soil and cut yields. 2. Tolliver's one field had a great year. → So the warning is overstated. This is the anecdote-versus-trend flaw (a hasty generalization from one case). It's a classic; know it. It's like: my uncle smoked and lived to 90, so the risks of smoking are exaggerated. We need an answer that says the farmer uses a single case to knock down a general claim.

choices.note: Polar vs. logical opposite. The farmer never says the practice improves soil; he only claims the harm is overstated. 'Not harmful' is not the same as 'beneficial.'
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Since this fertilizer doesn't damage the roots, it must make the plants grow faster.

choices.note: Tempting. Doubting a neighbor's brag feels natural. But nothing suggests Tolliver exaggerated, and even a perfectly accurate report of one harvest can't overturn a general warning. You can't pick an answer on a possibility.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: My cousin says his tomato plants never got blight, so blight must be rare. (trusts a possibly biased report)

choices.note: Wrong dimension. The argument is about soil and yields, not about cost. Cost is never in play.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Planting corn every year is the best choice for Tolliver, since soil depletion is minor. (ignores what rotation would cost)

choices.note: CORRECT. One field doing well says almost nothing about what generally happens across many fields. This is the anecdote-versus-trend flaw.
Wrong group. The warning is explicitly about corn, and Tolliver grows corn. There's no mismatch of crops to overlook.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Experts say wheat drains the soil, but my barley field is fine, so the experts are wrong.

questions.stimulus: Editor: For forty years, the Harlow Courier has printed a weekly list of local court filings. Recently some readers have urged the paper to drop the list, calling it an invasion of privacy. The Courier should keep printing it. Court filings are public records that anyone may inspect, so printing them reveals nothing truly private. Moreover, the list is the only regular source of this information for residents who cannot get to the courthouse.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the overall conclusion drawn in the editor's argument?
choices: Residents who cannot get to the courthouse have no other way to find out what court filings have been made.
Some of the Courier's readers have urged the paper to drop its list of court filings because printing it invades privacy.
The Courier's weekly list is the best available source of information about local court filings for most residents.
Printing the weekly list reveals nothing that is truly private, since the filings it reports are public records open to anyone.
The Courier ought to go on publishing its weekly list of court filings despite some readers' objections.
questions.explanation: After a background sentence and the readers' objection, the editor states the position: the Courier should keep printing the list. The public-records point supports 'reveals nothing truly private', and that claim and the only-source point both support keeping the list, so (E) is the main conclusion. (D) is the trap: it is flagged with 'so' in the stimulus, but it is a subsidiary conclusion offered as support. (C) turns 'only regular source' into an unsupported ranking.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The Courier should keep printing the list of court filings.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Filings are public records, so printing them reveals nothing truly private; the list is the only regular source for residents who can't reach the courthouse.

breakdown.analysis: Does the first sentence matter? No. 'For forty years the Courier has printed the list' is background; ignore it. Ask which statement supports which. The conclusion is the one everything else supports. 1. Filings are public records → printing them reveals nothing truly private. 2. The list is the only regular source for residents who can't reach the courthouse. Both 1 and 2 answer 'why keep the list?' Watch the 'so' in the middle: it marks a subsidiary conclusion (nothing truly private), not the main one. The main conclusion sits with no indicator at all, right after the objection: the Courier should keep printing it.

choices.note: Too broad. The editor says the list is the only regular source for these residents, not that they have no way at all to learn of the filings. And even the accurate version is a premise, not the conclusion.
This is the objection the editor is answering. Restating the opposing view is background, never the editor's conclusion.
Unsupported ranking. 'Only regular source for residents who can't get to the courthouse' is not 'best source for most residents.' The LSAT is ultra specific about words like best.

Tempting. It has its own 'so' in the stimulus, which makes it look like the conclusion. But it's a subsidiary conclusion: it's drawn from the public-records point and then offered, along with the only-source point, as a reason to keep printing the list. The main conclusion is what both reasons support.
CORRECT. This is the editor's position, and both later reasons (public records; the only regular source) are offered for it.

questions.stimulus: After the Eastgate branch library began offering Saturday story hours, it lent more children's books in a single year than it had ever lent before. Yet in that same year, for the first time in a decade, Eastgate was not the branch of the city library system that lent the most children's books.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above?
choices: Most of the children who attended Eastgate's Saturday story hours had already had library cards before the program ever began.
That year another branch doubled its children's collection, and its lending of children's books rose far more than Eastgate's.
For the decade before the story hours began, Eastgate lent more children's books each year than any other branch in the system did.
Eastgate's Saturday story hours drew larger audiences in their first year than any program the branch had offered before.
Children's books lent by Eastgate are, on average, returned later than children's books lent by the other branches.
questions.explanation: The puzzle confuses 'more than before' with 'the most of any branch'; Eastgate can set its own record while another branch grows even faster, which is exactly what (B) describes. (D) explains only the unpuzzling half (why Eastgate's lending rose), and (C) merely restates that Eastgate used to lead.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: Eastgate lent more children's books than ever, but it lost its spot as the branch lending the most children's books.

breakdown.analysis: How can Eastgate lend more than ever and still lose first place? Easy: 'more than before' is a relative word; 'the most' is a ranking against every other branch. This relative-vs-absolute switch is a classic paradox engine; know it. A runner can set a personal record and still finish second. We need an answer that says another branch grew even faster.

choices.note: Irrelevant. Whether story-hour kids already had cards doesn't explain why another branch passed Eastgate.
CORRECT. Eastgate went up, but another branch went up more and passed it. Both facts now fit.
This just restates the setup ('for the first time in a decade'). It makes losing first place more surprising, not less. It deepens the puzzle instead of resolving it.
Tempting. Big story-hour crowds explain why Eastgate's lending rose. But that's the half of the puzzle that isn't puzzling; nothing here says why another branch passed Eastgate.
Wrong dimension. How late books come back has nothing to do with how many are lent.

questions.stimulus: Last quarter, Kerrow Market offered shoppers free samples of its new house-brand granola at the store entrance. Of the roughly 2,000 shoppers who took a sample, 40 percent bought a box of the granola during that same visit. So the sampling stand is an effective way to boost sales of the granola.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument?
choices: Shoppers who took a sample were more likely than other shoppers to describe the store's prices overall as quite reasonable.
Shoppers who declined a sample tended to spend less in total during their visit than did shoppers who took one.
Shoppers who are never offered free samples at the store sometimes buy food products there that they have never tasted.
Throughout the quarter, the granola was priced well below comparable brands of granola sold at the store.
Under 5 percent of shoppers who declined a sample that quarter bought the granola on that visit.
questions.explanation: A 40 percent purchase rate among samplers means nothing without knowing the rate among shoppers who did not sample; (E) supplies that comparison group and shows a huge gap. (D) points the wrong way: a low price is an alternative reason many shoppers bought the granola, so it weakens rather than strengthens.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The sampling stand effectively boosts granola sales.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: 40 percent of shoppers who took a sample bought the granola that day.

breakdown.analysis: 40 percent compared to what? If 40 percent of shoppers who never tasted it also bought a box, the stand did nothing. The argument looks at only one group. This is the missing-comparison-group flaw; it's everywhere on the LSAT, so know it. It's like saying a tutor works because 80 percent of her students passed, without asking how many students passed overall. We need an answer that says shoppers who didn't sample bought the granola far less often.

choices.note: Wrong dimension. Opinions about prices aren't granola sales. This doesn't show the samples made anyone buy granola.
Wrong dimension again: total spending, not granola. And it could just mean bigger spenders like free food. It says nothing about whether sampling caused granola purchases.
Wrong group and irrelevant. Shoppers who are never offered samples sometimes buying untasted foods tells you nothing about this stand.

Tempting, because a low price sounds like a reason sales were good. But that's the problem: it's a different reason shoppers bought the granola, competing with the sampling explanation. If anything, it weakens.
CORRECT. This supplies the missing comparison group. 40 percent of samplers versus under 5 percent of decliners in the same quarter makes the stand look like it really drives sales.

questions.stimulus: Each summer, at least a few of the public beaches along the Ottery coast have water that is unsafe for swimming. The Ottery tourism office recommends a beach to visitors only if the office does not know the beach's water to be unsafe. This summer the office recommended every public beach on the coast.
questions.stem: The statements above, if true, most strongly support which one of the following?
choices: The tourism office does not test the water at the coast's public beaches before recommending them to visitors.
Most of the beaches that the tourism office recommended this summer had water that was unsafe for swimming.
Beaches known to have unsafe water cannot be recommended to visitors by any organization along the Ottery coast.
At least one beach the tourism office recommended this summer had unsafe water that the office was unaware of.
Unsafe water at a few beaches does not reduce the number of visitors to the Ottery coast enough to concern the office.
questions.explanation: Some beaches had unsafe water this summer, and the office recommended all of them while recommending only beaches it did not know to be unsafe; so at least one unsafe beach was unsafe without the office's knowledge, which is (D). (A) is merely possible: the office may test the water and simply miss a problem.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1) Every summer, at least a few Ottery beaches have unsafe water; 2) the office recommends a beach only if it doesn't know the beach's water is unsafe; 3) this summer it recommended every beach.

breakdown.analysis: Hard to fully prephrase, but combine the facts and something drops out. 1. This summer, at least a few beaches had unsafe water. 2. Recommended → the office didn't know the water was unsafe. 3. It recommended every beach. Chain: unsafe beach → recommended (3) → office didn't know it was unsafe (2). So unsafe-but-unknown beaches exist. Two facts like these force an existence inference. Watch for answers that guess at why it didn't know, or that inflate 'a few' to 'most.'

choices.note: Tempting. 'They didn't know' makes it feel like they didn't look. But the office could test carefully and still miss a problem. We don't know this.
Too strong. 'At least a few' unsafe beaches says nothing about most of them.
Wrong group and too broad. The rule is about this one office, not every organization on the coast.
CORRECT. Unsafe beaches existed this summer, the office recommended every beach, and it recommends only beaches it doesn't know to be unsafe. So at least one unsafe beach went unnoticed.
Wrong dimension and unsupported. The facts say nothing about visitor numbers or what concerns the office.

questions.stimulus:
Ines: The Ferndale Public Library should keep its reading room open until midnight during exam season. Students need a quiet place to study late that costs them nothing, and the library is the only such place in town.

Daniel: Students do need a quiet, free place to study late. But staying open until midnight would mean paying library staff overtime from an already strained budget. The school district's study hall, which also stays open late and is free, should fill that role instead.
questions.stem: Ines and Daniel disagree over whether
choices: the library should keep its reading room open until midnight during exam season
paying library staff overtime would place a strain on the library's already limited budget
the school district's study hall offers a quieter place to study than the library does
students would actually make use of the library's reading room if it stayed open until midnight during exam season
students need a quiet place to study late at night that costs them nothing to use
questions.explanation: Ines wants the reading room open until midnight; Daniel says the study hall should fill that role instead, so they disagree over (A). (E) is the trap: Daniel explicitly grants that students need a quiet, free place to study late, so that is a point of agreement.

setup.label: Arguments
setup.text: Ines: keep the library open until midnight; students need a free, quiet late-night spot and the library is the only one.; Daniel: yes, students need that, but overtime strains the budget; the district's free study hall should do it instead.

breakdown.analysis: Where does each speaker say yes and the other say no? To disagree, one speaker must say yes and the other no. Daniel's first sentence is a concession: 'Students do need a quiet, free place to study late.' So that's shared ground, not a dispute. Then he rejects Ines's plan: the study hall 'should fill that role instead.' That 'instead' is his no to her yes. We need the library-open-until-midnight point.

choices.note: CORRECT. Ines says yes in her first sentence. Daniel says the study hall should fill that role instead, so he says no. One yes, one no.
Only Daniel speaks to this. Ines never mentions overtime or the budget. One speaker silent means no disagreement.
Neither speaker compares how quiet the two places are. Daniel says the study hall should fill the role, not that it's quieter. Unsupported ranking.
Tempting. Ines's plan presupposes students would come. But Daniel never questions that; his objections are cost and the study hall alternative. One speaker silent means no disagreement.
Tempting, because both speakers talk about it. But that's the problem: they both say yes. Daniel opens by conceding exactly this. Agreement, not disagreement.

questions.stimulus: Critic: The Wexford Players' managing director claims that moving the company's season from the downtown hall to the new riverside venue will increase ticket sales, because the riverside venue has ample parking. But city surveys show that theatergoers rarely cite parking as a reason for staying home. It follows that the move will not increase ticket sales.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the critic's argument is flawed in that the argument
choices: treats evidence undermining the director's stated rationale as if it showed that the director's prediction is mistaken
relies on surveys whose respondents may not have been representative of the city's theatergoers in general
presumes, without providing justification, that whatever does not reduce attendance at a theater must increase it
infers that a reason offered in support of a claim is weak merely because that claim is false
concludes that the company should not move to the new venue on the basis of evidence about parking alone
questions.explanation: The critic undercuts the director's reason (parking) and then concludes the director's prediction is wrong, but the move could raise sales for other reasons, such as a larger hall or a more attractive location; (A) names this. (D) uses the familiar wording but runs the inference backward: the critic reasons from a weak reason to a false claim, not from a false claim to a weak reason. (E) is tempting, but the critic never says the move should not be made, only that it won't raise sales.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The move to the riverside venue will not increase ticket sales.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The director's reason was parking; surveys say parking rarely keeps people home.

breakdown.analysis: So the parking reason is weak. Does that mean sales won't rise? No. The new venue could sell more tickets for a dozen other reasons: a nicer setting, more seats, a busier neighborhood. You might think the flaw is that the survey is shaky. But even with a perfect survey, the critic only knocks down one reason. Treating a failed argument as proof that its conclusion is false is a classic flaw; know it. It's like: 'You say this restaurant is good because it's cheap? Price doesn't matter, so the restaurant is bad.' We need an answer that says the critic treats knocking down the director's reason as disproving the director's prediction. Note the correct answer doesn't use the stock wording; one wrong answer does.

choices.note: CORRECT. The surveys undercut the director's rationale (parking). The critic then treats that as showing the prediction itself is wrong. A weak reason doesn't make the claim false.
Merely possible. Nothing suggests the surveys were skewed. Even with perfect surveys, the real flaw remains.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: We polled visitors at the opera house, and most prefer opera, so the city's residents prefer opera to musicals.

choices.note: Polar vs. logical opposite, and the critic never reasons this way. Nobody here jumps from 'doesn't reduce' to 'increases.'
choices.example: Example of this flaw: The new lobby won't hurt attendance, so it is sure to boost attendance.

choices.note: Tempting, because it sounds like the textbook description of this flaw. But read the direction: it says the critic starts from 'the claim is false' and concludes 'the reason is weak.' The critic does the reverse: shows the reason is weak (surveys), then concludes the claim is false. Right words, wrong relation.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: The new stadium didn't bring in more fans, so the mayor's argument that it would attract tourists must have been a bad one.

choices.note: Tempting. It sounds like the critic's attitude. But the conclusion is only that sales won't rise, not that the move shouldn't happen. It adds a consequence the critic never draws.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Parking won't boost sales, so the company must not move.

questions.stimulus: For years, the Arvik research station measured air temperature with sensors mounted on the roof of its heated main building. In 2019 the sensors were moved to an open field 200 meters away, and the station's average recorded winter temperature since then has been 0.8°C lower than in the previous five winters. Thus, heat escaping from the building had been inflating the earlier readings.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?
choices: Sensors mounted on the roofs of heated buildings sometimes record air temperatures that are higher than those of the surrounding air.
The sensors installed in the open field in 2019 are a newer and more sensitive model than those used on the roof.
Summer temperatures recorded at the Arvik station, both before and after 2019, have varied considerably from year to year.
In 2013 the main building's roof was rebuilt with insulation so effective that almost no heat has escaped through it since.
Several other research stations in the region have also moved their sensors away from heated buildings in recent years.
questions.explanation: The argument blames escaping building heat for the higher pre-2019 readings, which requires that heat was actually escaping at the roof sensors during the comparison winters; (D) says that from 2013 on almost no heat escaped through the roof, so building heat cannot explain why 2014-2018 readings ran higher, and something else must account for the 0.8°C drop. (B) is tempting, but a newer model only weakens if we add the unstated assumption that it reads lower.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Building heat had been inflating the old rooftop readings.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: After the sensors moved away from the building in 2019, recorded winter averages dropped 0.8°C.

breakdown.analysis: Colder readings after the move. But was the building actually leaking heat onto the roof sensors in the five winters being compared? If not, building heat can't be what made those readings high. Structure: 1. Sensors moved from roof to field in 2019. 2. Winter averages since are 0.8°C lower than the previous five winters. → Building heat had inflated old readings. The argument needs its proposed mechanism to have been operating. We need an answer that knocks out the mechanism: no heat was escaping during the comparison period.

choices.note: Opposite direction. This makes the scientist's explanation more plausible. It strengthens.
Tempting. A new sensor model sounds like an alternative explanation. But nothing says the new model reads lower; you'd have to assume that. Merely possible.
Wrong group (summer, not winter) and a vague word ('varied'). Year-to-year summer swings don't explain a steady winter drop.

CORRECT. The comparison winters are 2014 to 2018. If the roof was rebuilt in 2013 so that almost no heat escaped, there was no building heat inflating those readings. The cause the argument names wasn't operating, so the drop needs some other explanation.
Wrong group. Other stations moving their sensors tells you nothing about what explains Arvik's numbers.

questions.stimulus: The Hollins Street Clinic is considering moving to the new Brookfield medical park. A clinic that moves will keep its regular patients only if those patients can easily reach its new location. All of the clinic's regular patients live in the Hollins Street neighborhood, and none of them drives. So if the clinic moves to the Brookfield medical park, it will not keep its regular patients.
questions.stem: The conclusion of the argument follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?
choices: If a clinic's regular patients can easily reach its new location, the clinic will keep those regular patients.
Most of the clinic's regular patients would prefer that the clinic remain at its current location on Hollins Street.
The Brookfield medical park is considerably farther from the Hollins Street neighborhood than the clinic's current location is.
The Brookfield medical park cannot easily be reached by residents of the Hollins Street neighborhood who do not drive.
Most of the patients who visit the clinics now located at the Brookfield medical park arrive there by car.
questions.explanation: Keep regulars → regulars can easily reach the new site. Contrapositive: can't easily reach → won't keep. The premises say the regulars live in the neighborhood and don't drive, so (D), which says such people can't easily reach Brookfield, completes the chain. (A) reverses the rule, and (C) is the near-miss: 'farther' is not the same as 'not easy to reach.'

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: If the clinic moves to Brookfield, it will not keep its regular patients.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Keeps regulars → regulars can easily reach the new site; all regulars live in the Hollins Street neighborhood and none drives.

breakdown.analysis: Why couldn't they reach Brookfield? Nothing yet says Brookfield is hard to get to. Chain: keeps regulars → regulars can easily reach new site. Contrapositive: regulars can't easily reach → doesn't keep them. We know who the regulars are (neighborhood residents, no cars). We need: neighborhood residents without cars → can't easily reach Brookfield. Then the chain runs straight to the conclusion. A sufficient assumption has to close the gap completely; 'farther' or 'most' won't do it.

choices.note: This reverses the rule: 'can reach → keep.' Even if true, it can't show the clinic will NOT keep its patients.
Preferences aren't access. Patients can prefer the old site and still follow the clinic if they can get there easily. The rule turns only on whether they can easily reach it.
Tempting. Farther sounds like harder to reach. But a farther site can still be easy to reach (a direct bus line, for example). It leaves the gap open.
CORRECT. Regulars = neighborhood residents who don't drive → can't easily reach Brookfield → clinic won't keep them. The conclusion follows.
So? How other clinics' patients arrive says nothing about whether non-drivers can easily get there. 'Most arrive by car' doesn't mean it's hard to arrive any other way.

questions.stimulus: Historian: In the decade after the lord of Staverley abolished the toll charged at the town gate in 1612, the number of merchants trading at Staverley's weekly market doubled. Some historians credit the toll's abolition for this. But nearly all of the newly arrived merchants came from Staverley itself or from nearby villages whose residents had always been exempt from the toll. So the abolition was not the main cause of the market's growth.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the historian's argument depends?
choices: The added merchants were not drawn mainly by an influx of buyers who had previously been kept away by the toll.
Merchants from the villages near Staverley did not need to pass through the town gate in order to reach the market.
Before 1612, few if any merchants from distant towns had traded at the weekly market in Staverley.
No other change that made Staverley's market easier to reach took place during the decade after 1612.
The lord of Staverley did not abolish the toll chiefly in order to enlarge the town's weekly market.
questions.explanation: The historian reasons that because the new merchants never paid the toll, ending the toll can't explain their arrival. That ignores an indirect route: ending the toll could have brought in buyers who did pay it, and those buyers could have drawn the exempt merchants. (A) rules that route out; negate it and the abolition becomes the main cause after all. (D) is the trap: another new attraction would support the historian's conclusion, so the argument doesn't need to deny one.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Abolishing the toll was not the main cause of the market's growth.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Merchants doubled after the toll ended; nearly all the new merchants came from places that were always exempt from the toll.

breakdown.analysis: So the new merchants never paid the toll. Does that mean the toll didn't matter to them? Not necessarily. Who else came through the gate? Buyers. If ending the toll brought a flood of shoppers, merchants would follow the shoppers, toll or no toll. Structure: 1. Toll abolished in 1612. 2. Merchants doubled. 3. The new merchants were exempt anyway. → Abolition wasn't the main cause. The argument only looks at the direct effect on merchants and ignores an indirect effect through buyers. It's like saying a new parking garage didn't help a mall's shops because the shop owners all live within walking distance. The right answer will be a defender that blocks the indirect route. Negate each choice and see which one breaks the argument.

choices.note: CORRECT. Negate it: the new merchants came mainly because buyers once deterred by the toll now flooded in. Then the abolition was the main cause, just indirectly, and the conclusion fails.
choices.negation: The added merchants were drawn mainly by an influx of buyers who had previously been kept away by the toll.

choices.note: Tempting, because it sounds like it keeps the villagers clear of the toll. But they were exempt anyway, so whether they passed the gate doesn't matter. Negating it changes nothing.
choices.negation: Village merchants did need to pass through the town gate. (They were exempt, so the toll still never touched them; argument survives.)

choices.note: Irrelevant to the argument's logic. The new merchants were local, whatever distant merchants did before 1612.
choices.negation: Before 1612, a fair number of distant merchants traded at the market. (Doesn't affect who the new merchants were; argument survives.)

choices.note: Tempting. It looks like a standard defender. But it points the wrong way: another new attraction would be a rival cause, which would help the historian's claim that the toll wasn't the main cause. The argument doesn't need to rule it out.
choices.negation: Some other change made the market easier to reach. (That would support the conclusion, not sink it.)
choices.example: Example of an argument that WOULD need this: The market grew after the toll ended, so ending the toll caused the growth.

choices.note: Motive is irrelevant. What the lord intended has no bearing on what actually caused the growth.
choices.negation: The lord did abolish the toll mainly to enlarge the market. (Intent doesn't make it the cause; argument survives.)

questions.stimulus: Five years ago, the managers of Ranmoor Reservoir banned motorboats there, because the boats' wakes often flooded the nests of loons along the shore. No loon nest at the reservoir has been flooded by a wake since the ban took effect. Yet the number of loon pairs nesting at the reservoir has declined every year since then.
questions.stem: Each of the following, if true, helps to explain why the number of loon pairs nesting at Ranmoor Reservoir has declined since the ban EXCEPT:
choices: Loon pairs whose nests are flooded early in the season usually build new nests within weeks and still raise chicks.
Motorboat traffic had kept away the gulls that raid loon nests for eggs, and gulls have returned to the shoreline since the ban.
Since the ban, far more hikers and anglers have used the shoreline, and loons often abandon their nests when people come near them.
Over the past five years, a disease has sharply reduced the numbers of the small fish on which the reservoir's loons feed their chicks.
Over the same period, nesting loon pairs have declined by a similar proportion throughout the region, including on lakes that still allow motorboats.
questions.explanation: Four choices give a reason the nesting population could fall even after wakes stopped flooding nests: returning egg predators (B), more human disturbance (C), less food (D), or a regional cause unrelated to boats (E). (A) is the exception: it shows that flooded nests were not much of a loss, which explains why the ban brought no gain, but it gives no reason for an actual decline.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: Motorboats, whose wakes flooded loon nests, were banned and no nest has been flooded since, but the number of nesting loon pairs has fallen every year.

breakdown.analysis: In an EXCEPT question, four answers do the job and one doesn't. So test each choice: does it give a reason the number of nesting pairs went DOWN? Not just 'why the ban didn't help,' but why things got worse. Watch that difference. An answer can explain why a fix failed to produce a gain without explaining a loss. That is the trap built into this question, and it's the answer.

choices.note: CORRECT. This explains why stopping the floods didn't produce more loons (flooded pairs re-nest anyway). But it says nothing about why numbers fell. 'No gain' isn't 'a decline.'

Helps explain. Surprising, but it works: the boats had a hidden benefit (keeping egg-raiding gulls away), and removing the boats removed that protection. A defect that turns out to help is a classic paradox resolver.
Helps explain. The ban brought a new source of disturbance, and disturbed loons abandon nests.
Helps explain. Less food for chicks plausibly means fewer pairs nesting, a cause that has nothing to do with boats.

Tempting to pick, because it seems to just describe the trend elsewhere. But it does explain: if loons are falling everywhere, even where boats remain, some regional cause is at work, and Ranmoor is caught up in it.

questions.stimulus: Researcher: Some argue that the ice cores drilled at the Tarn Glacier last decade are too shallow to reveal anything about climate before the last ice age. That is true, but it misses the point of the project. The cores were drilled to record the past few thousand years, and they record that period in exceptional detail, since their annual layers are thick enough to be counted one by one. So the project should be judged a success.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the role played in the researcher's argument by the claim that the cores record the past few thousand years in exceptional detail?
choices: It is the main conclusion of the argument, which the other claims in the argument are offered to support.
It is supported by another claim in the argument and is itself offered as support for the argument's main conclusion.
It is a claim that the researcher concedes is true but argues is irrelevant to evaluating the project.
It is offered as evidence that the cores also reveal something about the climate before the last ice age.
It is a premise offered in support of the claim that the cores' annual layers can be counted one by one.
questions.explanation: The claim about exceptional detail is supported by the countable annual layers ('since...') and in turn supports the main conclusion that the project should be judged a success, so it is an intermediate conclusion, as (B) says. (E) reverses the direction of support: the countable layers support the exceptional-detail claim, not the other way round.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The Tarn Glacier project should be judged a success.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Annual layers can be counted one by one → the cores record the past few thousand years in exceptional detail → that was the project's goal → success. (The 'too shallow' objection is conceded but set aside.)

breakdown.analysis: Which claim gets support, and which claim gives it? Follow the arrows. 1. Annual layers can be counted one by one ('since...') → 2. The cores record the past few thousand years in exceptional detail → 3. That was the project's goal → the project should be judged a success. The 'too shallow' objection is conceded and set aside. A claim that receives support and also gives support is an intermediate (subsidiary) conclusion. We need an answer that says exactly that.

choices.note: No. The last sentence, 'the project should be judged a success,' is the main conclusion. The detail claim supports it.
CORRECT. It's supported by the countable-layers claim ('since...') and in turn supports the conclusion that the project succeeded.
This describes the role of a different claim: the 'too shallow' objection, which the researcher concedes but sets aside. Right passage, wrong target.
Opposite. The researcher agrees the cores reveal nothing about pre-ice-age climate.
Tempting, since it connects the two claims correctly. But it runs the arrow backward: 'since' shows the countable layers support the detail claim, not the other way around.

questions.stimulus: The city's arborists follow this principle: a street tree should be removed at public expense if, but only if, a city arborist has inspected it within the past year and found either that it is diseased or that its roots are damaging a public sidewalk.
questions.stem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle stated above?
choices: An oak whose roots are cracking a sidewalk should be removed at public expense, even though a city arborist last inspected it fourteen months ago.
A maple that a city arborist found diseased last month should not be removed, since its roots are nowhere near a public sidewalk.
An ash should be removed at public expense, since an arborist hired by the homeowner, not a city arborist, found it diseased last month.
An elm that a city arborist found healthy and clear of the sidewalk last month should not be removed, despite a neighbor's complaints.
A sycamore that a city arborist has just found healthy should be removed, since its roots will probably reach the sidewalk within a few years.
questions.explanation: Remove ⇔ city arborist inspection within a year AND (diseased OR roots damaging a sidewalk). The elm in (D) was inspected last month by a city arborist who found neither condition, so the 'only if' half says not to remove it; the neighbor's complaints don't count. (B) is the trap: a recent city inspection found disease, so the 'if' half requires removal even though the roots are harmless.

setup.label: Principle
setup.text: Remove at public expense ⇔ a city arborist inspected it within the past year AND found (diseased OR roots damaging a public sidewalk).

setup.label: Application
setup.text: Find the judgment whose remove/keep decision matches the rule.

breakdown.analysis: 'If, but only if' runs both ways. 'If': inspected by a city arborist within a year and found diseased or damaging → must remove. 'Only if': no such finding → must not remove. So check three things in every choice: who inspected (a city arborist?), when (within a year?), and what was found (disease or sidewalk damage?). And remember the rule cuts both ways: a 'kept' judgment can conform too. It's easy to hunt for the right removal and skip the right decision not to remove.

choices.note: Fails the timing condition. Fourteen months is more than a year, so the rule does not permit removal, even though the roots really are cracking the sidewalk.

Tempting, because people read the 'or' as an 'and.' Disease alone is enough: a city arborist found it diseased last month, so the principle says remove it. 'Should not be removed' violates the 'if' half.
Fails the inspector condition. The rule requires a city arborist; a homeowner's arborist doesn't count, so removal at public expense isn't permitted.

CORRECT. A city arborist inspected it last month and found neither disease nor sidewalk damage, so the 'only if' half says it should not be removed. A neighbor's complaints aren't a city arborist's finding.
Fails the finding condition. 'Will probably reach the sidewalk' isn't 'is damaging a sidewalk,' and the tree was found healthy. Removal isn't permitted.

questions.stimulus: To save on wages, Pellam's Home Supply plans to staff fewer checkout lanes on weekday mornings, when few customers shop. But many of its weekday-morning customers are contractors buying supplies in bulk before work, and contractors are the store's biggest spenders. So the plan risks costing Pellam's more in lost sales than it saves in wages.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the argument depends?
choices: Contractors who shop at Pellam's account for most of the store's total sales over the course of a year.
Weekday-morning wages make up at least a significant portion of what Pellam's pays its checkout staff over a typical week.
Longer weekday-morning checkout waits would lead at least some contractors to spend less at Pellam's than they otherwise would.
Pellam's managers have not seriously considered reducing checkout staffing at other times of the week instead.
At least some customers who shop at other times of the week are less bothered by long checkout lines than contractors are.
questions.explanation: The predicted lost sales only happen if the reduced staffing actually drives some contractors to spend less; negate (C) (no contractor would buy less despite longer waits) and the risk disappears. (A) is the too-strong trap: the contractors can be the store's biggest spenders, and losing their business can be costly, without their making up most of total sales. (B) and (E) are hedged like typical assumptions, but negating either leaves the argument untouched.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The staffing cut risks losing more in sales than it saves in wages.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Many weekday-morning shoppers are contractors, the biggest spenders.

breakdown.analysis: Big spenders shop on weekday mornings. So what? Do they actually buy less if the lines get longer? If they wait patiently and buy the same, nothing is lost. Structure: 1. Fewer lanes on weekday mornings. 2. Many of those shoppers are contractors, the biggest spenders. → Risk of losing more in sales than saved in wages. Missing link: the longer waits cause some contractors to spend less. Necessary assumptions are usually modest ('at least some'). Negate each choice and see which one breaks the argument.

choices.note: Tempting. If contractors are the biggest spenders, they sound like most of the business. But being the biggest spenders doesn't mean making up most of total sales, and the argument works either way. Too strong.
choices.negation: Contractors do not account for most of Pellam's total sales. (Losing some of them could still cost more than the wage savings; argument survives.)

choices.note: Hedged like a real assumption, but not needed. If weekday-morning wages were only a small portion of checkout pay, the wage savings would be smaller, which makes the argument's risk of lost sales outweighing the savings even more likely.
choices.negation: Weekday-morning wages make up only a small portion of checkout pay. (If anything, this helps the argument.)

choices.note: CORRECT. Negate it: no contractor would spend any less, however long the wait. Then there are no lost sales, and the argument collapses.
choices.negation: Longer weekday-morning checkout waits would not lead any contractors to spend less at Pellam's.

choices.note: Irrelevant. What managers have or haven't considered elsewhere doesn't affect this plan's risk.
choices.negation: Pellam's managers have seriously considered reducing staffing at other times. (No effect.)

choices.note: Hedged, but wrong group. How shoppers at other times feel about lines has nothing to do with whether contractors on weekday mornings will spend less.
choices.negation: No customers who shop at other times are less bothered by lines than contractors. (No effect.)

questions.stimulus: Every one of the 140 employees of the Danvers customer-service call center completed an anonymous self-evaluation last month. One question asked employees to compare their own patience with callers to that of the center's other employees. Most of the employees reported that they are more patient with callers than most of their coworkers at the center are.
questions.stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must also be true?
choices: Most of the employees who made that report are not in fact more patient with callers than most of their coworkers.
Not every employee who made that report is in fact more patient with callers than most coworkers.
No employee at the center could have known whether he or she is more patient with callers than most coworkers are.
Employees who are more patient with callers tend to receive fewer complaints from callers than less patient employees do.
Most of the center's employees are less patient with callers than the center's own training guidelines recommend.
questions.explanation: Rank all 140 employees by patience: only those in the top half (at most 70) can each be more patient than most of their 139 coworkers. Yet more than half (at least 71) reported being so, so at least one report must be false, which (B) states as 'not every' report is accurate. (A) is the trap: if 71 made the report and 70 are truly that patient, only one report is false, not most. (C) overreaches into what employees could know.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1. All 140 employees answered the survey; 2. most (71+) reported being more patient with callers than most of their coworkers.

breakdown.analysis: Can most people each be more patient than most others? No. Line the 140 employees up from most to least patient. To beat most of your 139 coworkers you must beat at least 70 of them, so only the top 70 qualify, and ties only shrink that number. But 71 or more said they qualify. So at least one of them is wrong. That's all we know: maybe just one. Most students pick (A) because 'most people overrate themselves' is the familiar story and the numbers seem to point there. But with 71 reports and 70 true qualifiers, only one report is false. 'At least one' isn't 'most.' We need the modest answer, and here it's dressed in a 'not every' negative.

choices.note: Tempting. It's the cynical story the stimulus seems to tell. But the math only forces one false report. If 71 reported and 70 qualify, 70 of the 71 are right. Too strong.
CORRECT. 'Not every' = at least one is not. At most 70 can truly be more patient than most coworkers, and 71+ said so, so at least one report is inaccurate.
Too strong. Some employees could know perfectly well; the facts only show that at least one report is wrong, not that no one could know.
New information. The stimulus says nothing about complaints.
The training guidelines never appear. Out of scope.

questions.stimulus: Shipping firms that route cargo through the Corrish Strait rather than around the Kell Peninsula save four days of fuel and crew costs per voyage. Yet many firms still avoid the strait. The most likely reason is that insurers charge far higher premiums for voyages through the strait, enough to wipe out the savings from the shorter route.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument?
choices: The Corrish Strait is narrower and harder to navigate than most of the other shipping lanes in the region.
Pirate attacks on cargo ships passing through the Corrish Strait have become steadily more frequent over the past decade.
The few shipping firms that carry their own risk rather than buying insurance send nearly all of their cargo through the strait.
Insurers set their premiums for strait voyages chiefly according to the strait's record of groundings and collisions.
Insurers also charge higher premiums for voyages around the Kell Peninsula during the region's winter storm season.
questions.explanation: If premiums are what keeps firms out of the strait, firms that pay no premium should use it. (C) shows exactly that: the firms that carry their own risk send nearly all their cargo through. (D) is the trap: it is about insurers and premiums, but it ties the premiums to the strait's danger, which is a rival reason to avoid it. (B), piracy, is likewise a rival reason.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Firms avoid the Corrish Strait mainly because insurance premiums for it are high enough to cancel the time savings.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The strait saves four days, yet many firms avoid it.

breakdown.analysis: Premiums are the 'most likely reason'? Why not danger, narrow channels, or something else? Structure: 1. The strait saves four days. 2. Many firms avoid it anyway. → Because insurers charge premiums that wipe out the savings. A neat way to test a cause: find a group that lacks it. Who doesn't pay strait premiums? Firms that don't buy insurance at all. If they happily use the strait, the premium story looks right. Most students hunt for an answer about premiums being high and grab the insurer answer; read what it actually says about why premiums are high.

choices.note: Merely possible, and it points the wrong way. A hard-to-navigate strait is a competing reason to avoid it. It doesn't tie avoidance to premiums.

Tempting. Piracy might push premiums up, which sounds like support. But as stated it's a separate reason to avoid the strait (danger to ships and crews). You'd have to assume it works only through premiums. It weakens.

CORRECT. Firms that buy no insurance pay no premium, and they're exactly the ones that use the strait. Take away the premium and the avoidance disappears, which is what the argument predicts. It's a comparison group that differs only in the factor the argument blames.

Tempting. It mentions insurers and premiums, so it feels like support. But it says the premiums track how dangerous the strait is, which hands you a rival reason firms might stay away: the danger itself. It explains the premiums, not the avoidance.
Wrong group (the other route) and opposite direction. Higher premiums around the peninsula would make the strait relatively more attractive, deepening the puzzle.

questions.stimulus: Museum director: In 1924 a collector bought our carved screen from a villager who tended the village temple. By village custom, only the elders could sell temple property, and they never approved the sale, though no law then forbade it. The village now asks for the screen. Some trustees say a century of our careful keeping has made it ours. But careful keeping cannot cure a defective acquisition. We should return the screen.
questions.stem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the museum director's reasoning?
choices: Long and careful keeping of an object does not by itself give the keeper a right to retain that object.
An object acquired in accordance with the laws then in force should be returned only if the community it came from asks for it back.
Property transferred in breach of the owning community's own rules should be restored whenever that community asks for it back.
Objects taken from a community without the consent of any of its members should be returned to that community whenever it asks for them.
A museum should return any object whose acquisition would be illegal if the same transaction took place today.
questions.explanation: The director's case: by the village's own custom the sale was unauthorized; the village asks for the screen; legality then and a century of care don't settle the matter. (C) requires restoring property transferred in breach of the owning community's own rules whenever that community asks, regardless of what the law allowed, which yields the conclusion. (A) is the trap: it answers the trustees' objection but never says the screen should go back. (B) gives only a necessary condition for return, and (D) fails because the seller was a villager who consented.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The museum should return the screen to the village.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: A villager sold it, but by custom only the elders could, and they never approved; no law forbade the sale; the village asks for it; a century of care can't cure a defective acquisition.

breakdown.analysis: Why give back something no law stopped you from buying, and that you've cared for for a century? The director's answer has two parts: the sale was defective by the village's own rules, and the village is asking. So the principle must (1) make the village's custom, not the law, the test of whether the sale was proper, and (2) say an improper sale should be undone on request. Watch for answers that do only half: knocking down the trustees' objection isn't the same as telling you to return the screen. A principle-justify answer has to tell you to do what the conclusion says.

choices.note: Tempting. It's the director's rebuttal of the trustees, almost in the director's words. But removing one reason to keep the screen isn't a reason to return it. It clears an objection; it doesn't reach the conclusion.

Necessary vs. sufficient trap. 'Return only if asked' makes a request necessary for return. The village did ask, but meeting a necessary condition doesn't establish that the screen should be returned.

CORRECT. By the village's own rules the sale was a breach (only the elders could sell, and they didn't). Property transferred in breach of the community's rules should be restored when the community asks, and it has. That's the conclusion, and the law of 1924 drops out: the test is the community's rules, not the law.
Scope. 'Without the consent of ANY member' isn't met: the seller was a villager, and he obviously consented. One word sinks it.
We don't know this. The stimulus says no law then forbade the sale; it says nothing about today's law. A condition the facts don't establish can't justify the conclusion.

questions.stimulus: Dairy farms in Quill County that switched their herds to locally grown alfalfa last year saw average milk output per cow rise by 8 percent, while farms that kept their old feed saw no change. Therefore, any Quill County dairy farm that switches to locally grown alfalfa can expect its cows' milk output to rise.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?
choices: Locally grown alfalfa costs considerably more per ton than the feed that most Quill County dairy farms currently use.
Before switching, each farm that adopted alfalfa had been giving its cows a low-protein feed that no other Quill County farm uses.
A few of the farms that switched to alfalfa last year also replaced some of their older cows with younger, higher-yielding ones.
Among the farms that switched to alfalfa last year, the size of the increase in milk output per cow varied considerably.
Cows fed locally grown alfalfa produce milk with a slightly higher fat content than cows given other kinds of feed.
questions.explanation: The argument generalizes from the switching farms to any farm, but (B) shows the switchers differed from the rest: they were leaving a low-protein feed no other farm uses, so their gain may reflect escaping that feed rather than any benefit of alfalfa over ordinary feed. (C) is the trap: an alternative cause, but one limited to a few farms, so it can't explain the average rise or say anything about other farms.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Any Quill County farm that switches to local alfalfa can expect milk output to rise.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Farms that switched last year rose 8 percent; farms that didn't switch saw no change.

breakdown.analysis: So the switching farms improved. Will every farm improve? Only if the switchers were like everybody else. What if they started from a worse position? Structure: 1. Switchers' output rose 8 percent. 2. Non-switchers: no change. → Any farm that switches can expect a rise. The comparison group may differ in a way that matters. It's like: patients with a vitamin deficiency felt better after taking the vitamin, so everyone who takes it will feel better. We need an answer that shows the switchers' gain came from something that doesn't carry over to other farms.

choices.note: Wrong dimension. Cost isn't milk output. The argument only claims output will rise, not that switching pays off.

CORRECT. The switchers weren't typical: they were escaping a poor feed. Their gain may come from dropping that feed, not from alfalfa itself, so a farm already on ordinary feed has no reason to expect a rise.

Tempting: an alternative cause. But it covers only a few of the switching farms, so it can't account for the average rise across all of them, and it says nothing about whether farms that didn't switch would gain. It chips at the evidence; it doesn't undercut the generalization.
So? An average rise of 8 percent is compatible with some farms gaining more and others less. Variation doesn't show the feed didn't cause the rise.
Wrong dimension (fat content, not quantity), and if anything it's a small point in the feed's favor.

questions.stimulus: Dramaturg: Some critics define a 'repertory company' as any theater company that stages several different plays in a single season. But consider a company that stages five plays in a season, hiring a separate cast for each production and never reusing an actor. No one would call that a repertory company, since the hallmark of repertory is a stable group of actors who perform together across productions.
questions.stem: The dramaturg's argument proceeds by
choices: arguing that a proposed definition wrongly excludes some companies that have the trait central to the category being defined
describing a case that satisfies a proposed definition but lacks a trait that is central to the category being defined
appealing to a hypothetical case in order to show that the critics have applied their own definition inconsistently
showing that a proposed criterion implies that every theater company, whatever its practices, is a repertory company
replacing the critics' definition with one that he shows applies to every company to which the critics' definition applies
questions.explanation: The five-play company with a new cast for each production meets the critics' criterion (several plays in one season) yet lacks the stable group of actors that marks a repertory company, so the dramaturg shows the criterion lets in something it shouldn't: (B). (A) is the trap: it describes the opposite failure, a definition that is too narrow. (C) gets the hypothetical case right but invents an inconsistency.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The critics' definition of 'repertory company' (any company staging several plays in a season) is wrong.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: A company staging five plays with a new cast each time meets the definition but is not a repertory company, because repertory requires a stable group of actors.

breakdown.analysis: Does the dramaturg's example get left out by the definition, or let in? Let in: five plays in a season is 'several,' so it satisfies the critics' definition. But it lacks the hallmark, a stable cast. So the definition is too broad. A definition can fail two ways: too broad (includes non-members) or too narrow (excludes members). This is worth knowing for every definition question. Most students who miss this pick (A) because 'the definition is wrong because of a counterexample' is the prephrase, and (A) is a definition attack. But (A) is the too-narrow move. We need an answer that says: meets the definition, lacks the essential feature.

choices.note: Tempting. It's the classic definition attack, and it sounds right. But it's the too-narrow move: something that belongs gets left out. The dramaturg's company gets let IN by the definition and doesn't belong. That's too broad.
choices.example: Example of this method: Critics define a band as a group that plays original songs. But a group that plays only covers, rehearsing and touring together for years, is plainly a band.

choices.note: CORRECT. Five plays in a season satisfies 'several plays'; a new cast for each production lacks the stable group of actors that marks repertory. Meets the definition, isn't a member: too broad.

Half right. The dramaturg does use a hypothetical case. But he never shows the critics applying their definition one way here and another way there. He shows the definition itself gives the wrong result.
choices.example: Example of this method: The critics call the Elm Players a repertory company but deny that label to the Oak Players, though both stage several plays a season.

choices.note: Too strong. One company that the definition wrongly includes doesn't show that every company is included. A company staging a single play would still fail the definition.
choices.example: Example of this method: By the critics' definition, even a company that stages one play a year would count, and so would every other company.

choices.note: The dramaturg does mention the hallmark of repertory, but he doesn't show it covers everything the critics' definition covers. In fact his point is that it covers less.
choices.example: Example of this method: Instead of "several plays a season," define repertory as "a company that produces plays," which covers every company the old definition did.

questions.stimulus: The Climate Data Trust funds a research proposal only if the proposal guarantees that its data will be made public within a year of collection. No proposal that relies on data licensed from a private weather firm can make that guarantee, since such firms restrict publication. Dr. Okafor's proposal on coastal fog relies on data from the Merrin Observatory. So the Trust will not fund Dr. Okafor's proposal.
questions.stem: The conclusion of the argument can be properly drawn if which one of the following is assumed?
choices: If a proposal guarantees that its data will be made public within a year of collection, the Trust will fund it.
Most of the data that the Merrin Observatory provides to researchers is licensed from private weather firms.
The Merrin Observatory supplies researchers only with data that it has licensed from private weather firms.
Private weather firms restrict the publication of all of the data they collect, whether or not that data is licensed.
Dr. Okafor's proposal does not rely on any data that is already available to the public free of charge.
questions.explanation: Funded → guarantee; relies on privately licensed data → no guarantee. So the conclusion follows once Okafor's Merrin data counts as privately licensed data, and (C) supplies exactly that: everything Merrin supplies is licensed from private firms. (B) is the trap: it's the right idea at the wrong strength; if only most Merrin data is licensed, Okafor might rely solely on the unlicensed rest. (A) reverses the funding condition.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The Trust will not fund Dr. Okafor's proposal.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Funded → guarantees publication within a year; relies on privately licensed data → can't guarantee; Okafor relies on Merrin Observatory data.

breakdown.analysis: Why would Merrin data block funding? Nothing yet says Merrin data is licensed from a private firm. Chain: relies on privately licensed data → no guarantee → not funded. Okafor: relies on Merrin data → ??? We need: Merrin data → privately licensed data. Then Okafor → licensed → no guarantee → not funded. The right answer states that bridge without using the words 'proposal' or 'guarantee,' so it's easy to read past. Most students who miss this pick (B) because it names Merrin and private licensing together. But 'most' is too weak for a sufficient assumption: Okafor might use only the unlicensed part. You can't pick an SA answer that leaves a gap.

choices.note: This reverses the funding rule: guarantee → funded. Even if true, it can't show a proposal will NOT be funded.
Tempting. Right idea, wrong strength. If only most Merrin data is licensed, Okafor's proposal could rely entirely on the unlicensed remainder, and the conclusion wouldn't follow.
CORRECT. Merrin data → licensed from a private firm. Then: Okafor relies on licensed data → can't guarantee publication → not funded.
Says private firms restrict all their data, but still doesn't say Merrin data comes from a private firm. The gap remains.
Irrelevant. Whether Okafor uses freely available data doesn't link Merrin data to private licensing.

questions.stimulus: Last year an insurance company's appraisers examined every painting the company insured, flagging some as probable forgeries. Dealers in the Vashti district had sold 10 percent of the paintings examined, about their share of the region's art sales, yet 40 percent of the flagged paintings came from Vashti dealers. So a painting bought from a Vashti dealer is more likely to be a forgery than one bought from another dealer in the region.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the argument?
choices: Every painting that the appraisers flagged as a probable forgery last year was in fact a forgery.
Forgeries sold outside the Vashti district were not much less likely to be flagged by the appraisers than Vashti forgeries were.
The paintings that the appraisers examined last year included paintings sold by every dealer in the Vashti district.
Paintings sold by Vashti dealers are, on average, less expensive than paintings sold by other dealers in the region.
Most of the forged paintings sold in the region last year were sold by dealers outside the Vashti district.
questions.explanation: The argument reads the flagged paintings as a measure of where forgeries are. That works only if a forgery's chance of being caught didn't depend on where it was sold; if other dealers' forgeries were subtler, or got less scrutiny, they could be just as common yet rarely flagged. (B) rules this out; negate it and the 40 percent figure no longer tracks actual forgeries. (A) is the trap: it shores up the evidence but demands far more than needed, since flags can be imperfect as long as they err evenly across dealers.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: A painting from a Vashti dealer is more likely to be forged than one from another dealer in the region.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Vashti dealers sold 10 percent of the paintings examined but account for 40 percent of those flagged as probable forgeries.

breakdown.analysis: Flagged isn't the same as forged. Does the flagging catch forgeries equally well everywhere? Suppose Vashti forgers are clumsy and everyone else's are superb: Vashti fakes get caught, the others sail through, and the real forgery rates could be identical. The argument needs the detection rate to be roughly even across dealers. Notice the stimulus never mentions how good the appraisers are at catching different forgeries; the right answer defends against an alternative you have to invent yourself. Negate each choice: which negation breaks the link between 'flagged' and 'forged'?

choices.note: Tempting. It defends the step from 'flagged' to 'forged,' which is the real weak spot. But 'every' is far too strong. If 20 percent of flags were mistakes, spread evenly across dealers, the comparison would still hold.
choices.negation: At least one flagged painting was genuine. (A few errors, spread evenly, leave the comparison intact.)

choices.note: CORRECT. Negate it: other dealers' forgeries were much less likely to be caught. Then the 40 percent could reflect easy detection, not more forgeries, and the conclusion has no support.
choices.negation: Forgeries sold outside Vashti were much less likely to be flagged than Vashti forgeries.

choices.note: Sounds like a representativeness requirement, but the argument doesn't need every single Vashti dealer covered. A broad sample that missed one small dealer would do.
choices.negation: At least one Vashti dealer had no paintings examined. (The comparison can still hold.)

choices.note: Interesting fact, but not relevant. It might suggest a reason forgeries end up there, but the argument doesn't need any explanation of why.
choices.negation: Vashti paintings are not cheaper on average. (No effect on the comparison.)

choices.note: Tempting to treat as a problem, but it's perfectly consistent with the argument: Vashti sells only 10 percent of paintings, so other dealers can sell most forgeries while each Vashti painting is still likelier to be fake. Rate, not count.
choices.negation: Most forged paintings were sold by Vashti dealers. (That would only help the argument.)

questions.stimulus: A piano tuned by the Kestrel Piano Service will hold its tuning for at least six months if it is kept away from radiators. The Morrows' piano was tuned by Kestrel in January, but it sits right beside a radiator in their living room. So the Morrows' piano will not hold its tuning for six months.
questions.stem: Which one of the following arguments exhibits a flawed pattern of reasoning most similar to that exhibited by the argument above?
choices: A container shipped by Norrland Freight will arrive within a week only if it clears customs on its first inspection. One Norrland container failed its first customs inspection. So that container will not arrive within a week.

If a newspaper's investigative series wins a regional award, the paper's circulation rises the following year. The Gazette's circulation rose this year. So its investigative series must have won a regional award last year.
A tenant's lease will be renewed automatically if the tenant has paid every month's rent on time. Ms. Hale has paid every month's rent on time. So her lease will be renewed automatically.

The new floor cleaner has been shown not to harm hardwood finishes, and anything that does not harm hardwood finishes is safe to use every week. So the new cleaner must actually be good for hardwood finishes.

Joaquin, an apprentice with the Tallis company, has never completed the stage-combat course. Since completing that course is enough to clear any Tallis apprentice to perform fight scenes, Joaquin is not cleared to perform them.
questions.explanation: The argument treats being kept away from radiators as necessary for a Kestrel-tuned piano to hold its tuning, when it was stated only as sufficient (Kestrel tuning and no radiator → holds tuning; the Morrows' piano is near a radiator; so it won't hold). (E) states its condition with 'is enough to,' which is also only sufficient, and denies it in the same way, though its premises come in a different order. (A) is the trap: it reads almost word for word like the original, but its 'only if' makes clearing customs necessary, so denying it validly yields the conclusion. (B) is flawed in a different way (it affirms the result).

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The Morrows' piano will not hold its tuning for six months.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Kestrel tuning AND kept away from radiators → holds tuning 6+ months; the Morrows' piano was tuned by Kestrel but sits by a radiator.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: Members of group G with condition C get result R; this member of G lacks C; so this member won't get R. (Denying the sufficient condition.)

breakdown.analysis: The piano sits by a radiator. Does that doom its tuning? No: staying away from radiators was given as enough for the tuning to hold, not as required. Chain: Kestrel tuning AND away from radiators → holds 6+ months. Morrows: Kestrel tuning, beside a radiator. → Won't hold. That's denying the sufficient condition (treating a sufficient condition as necessary), a classic; know it. Most students pick (A) because it is nearly a word-for-word copy: 'will arrive within a week ... if it clears customs ... failed ... so will not arrive.' But one word changes everything: 'only if.' That makes clearing customs necessary, and denying a necessary condition is valid. A valid argument can't match a flawed one. The right answer hides its sufficient condition in 'is enough to' and puts its premises in a different order.

choices.note: Tempting. Same sentence shape and almost the same words. But 'will arrive ... only if it clears customs' makes clearing customs a necessary condition: arrives in a week → cleared. This container didn't clear, so it won't arrive in a week. That's valid.
Flawed, but a different flaw. It reverses the conditional: circulation rose → award, affirming the result instead of denying the condition.
Valid. On-time rent → renewal; Hale paid on time; so renewed. It affirms the sufficient condition, which is fine. No flaw to match.
A different flaw: it treats 'does not harm' as 'is good for' (polar vs. logical opposite). No conditional is being denied.

CORRECT. 'Is enough to clear' = completes the course → cleared (sufficient). Joaquin hasn't completed it, so 'not cleared.' Same mistake: the course is sufficient, not shown to be necessary. Don't be thrown by the order: the case comes first and the rule second, but the skeleton matches.

questions.stimulus: Scholar: It is often said that printing spread literacy in the towns of Lenmark because printed books cost far less than handwritten ones. They did cost less. But in the towns where presses arrived earliest, literacy rose only decades later, once the towns began paying for schools; and in towns with no press, literacy rose as soon as schools opened. Thus, ______.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most logically completes the scholar's argument?
choices: when literacy spread in Lenmark's towns depended more on access to instruction than on access to inexpensive reading matter
the printing press did nothing to spread literacy in the towns of Lenmark, despite the low cost of printed books
literacy cannot rise in a town unless that town pays for schools, whether or not it has a printing press
the towns where presses arrived earliest were slower than the towns without presses to begin paying for schools
inexpensive printed books helped spread literacy in Lenmark's towns only after those towns had begun paying for schools
questions.explanation: The scholar grants that printed books were cheaper but shows that literacy rose when schools appeared, whether or not cheap books had long been available. The supported completion is comparative: (A), the timing of literacy followed instruction more than cheap reading matter. (B) is the trap: it borrows the stimulus's words but turns 'not the main driver' into 'did nothing,' which the evidence can't show. (E) sounds like a moderate compromise, but nothing shows cheap books helped at all. (D) misreads 'decades later' as a comparison with the no-press towns, whose school dates are never given. (C) overreaches into a necessary condition for every town.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1) Popular view: cheap printed books spread literacy; 2) printed books were indeed cheaper; 3) early-press towns saw literacy rise only when schools were funded, decades later; 4) towns without presses saw literacy rise as soon as schools opened.

breakdown.analysis: 'It is often said ... But' signals a pushback, and the concession ('They did cost less') tells you the scholar isn't denying the premise, only the explanation. What tracks the rise in literacy? Schools, every time; cheap books sat around for decades with no effect. So the blank should say schooling mattered more than cheap books for when literacy spread.
