Expect traps that go too far (cheap books did NOTHING; schools are REQUIRED everywhere), traps that sound balanced but add a claim the evidence never makes (cheap books DID help, just later), and traps that compare things the facts never compare.

choices.note: CORRECT. Literacy rose when schools came, with or without long-available cheap books. That supports a comparison, instruction over inexpensive books, and nothing stronger. Abstract, but it's exactly the scholar's point.
Tempting, because it echoes the stimulus. But 'did nothing' is too strong. Cheap books might have helped once schools existed; the evidence shows only that they weren't what set the timing.
Too strong. A handful of towns where literacy followed schools doesn't show literacy can never rise without town-funded schools.

Tempting. 'Literacy rose only decades later' makes the early-press towns sound slow to fund schools. But slow compared to what? The scholar never says when the no-press towns opened their schools. The comparison isn't in the facts.

Tempting, because it sounds measured: it seems to split the difference between the popular view and the scholar's. But it asserts that cheap books DID help spread literacy, and nothing in the evidence shows that. The facts show only that literacy tracked schools. Possible, not supported.

questions.stimulus: The Ashcroft family papers, recently donated to the county historical society, consist mainly of letters. Most of the letters were written by the women of the family, and among the women's letters, those dealing chiefly with household accounts outnumber all the others combined. So most of the letters in the collection deal chiefly with household accounts.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument
choices: infers that most of the letters about household accounts were written by the women from the claim that most of the women's letters are about household accounts
takes for granted that the women of the family wrote no letters dealing chiefly with any subject other than household accounts
treats a feature that predominates within the larger part of a collection as if it must predominate within the collection as a whole
treats a feature that predominates within a collection as a whole as if it must predominate within the larger part of that collection
relies on a classification of the letters by subject that historians who study the Ashcroft family might reasonably dispute
questions.explanation: The women's letters are most of the collection, and account letters are most of the women's letters, but 'most of most' can be well under half of the whole (60 percent of letters by women, 58 percent of those about accounts, is about 35 percent of all letters); (C) describes this move from the larger part to the whole. (D) is the near-miss: same terms, but it runs from whole to part, the reverse of what the argument does. (A) describes a different quantifier reversal the argument never makes; the argument concludes something about all the letters, not about who wrote the account letters.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Most of the letters in the Ashcroft papers deal chiefly with household accounts.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Most of the letters were written by the women of the family; among the women's letters, account letters outnumber all the rest combined (that is, most of the women's letters are about accounts).

breakdown.analysis: First translate: 'outnumber all the others combined' just means MOST of the women's letters are about accounts. So: most letters are the women's, most of the women's are about accounts, so most letters are about accounts. Most of most = most? No. Try numbers: 100 letters, 60 by women, 35 of those about accounts. 35 is most of the women's letters and the women wrote most of the letters, but 35 is not most of 100. This quantifier slip is worth knowing. Structurally: a feature dominates the BIGGER PART, and the argument concludes it dominates the WHOLE. The right answer says exactly that, in abstract words, and two wrong answers are built to look like it: (D) uses the same words in the reverse direction (whole to part), and (A) describes a different quantifier reversal. Check direction: what was the premise about, and what was the conclusion about?

choices.note: Tempting. It's a real quantifier flaw (reversing 'most A are B' into 'most B are A'). But this argument never concludes that most account letters were by women; it concludes something about all the letters. Right kind of flaw, wrong argument.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Most of the club's runners are women, so most of the club's women are runners.

choices.note: Overstated. The argument says only that MOST of the women's letters are about accounts; it doesn't need all of them to be. Too strong to be what it takes for granted.

CORRECT. The 'larger part of the collection' is the women's letters; the 'feature' is dealing with household accounts. It predominates there, and the argument concludes it predominates in the whole collection. That doesn't follow: the remaining letters could swamp it.

Tempting. It's the key's wording with the direction flipped. The argument's premise is about the women's letters (the larger part) and its conclusion is about the whole collection: part to whole. This describes whole to part, which the argument never does.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Most of the library's books are fiction, and most of its books are in the main building, so most of the books in the main building are fiction.

choices.note: A premise objection. Questioning how letters were classified doesn't show a flaw in the reasoning; the inference fails even with a perfect classification.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Experts might classify these letters differently, so the conclusion about their subjects is wrong.

questions.stimulus: Council member: The proposed curfew for residents under eighteen would probably cut downtown vandalism somewhat, but that vandalism is rare and minor, and the curfew would bar hundreds of law-abiding young people from evening events. Some note that we already restrict young people in other ways, such as with a minimum driving age. But a driving age shields young people from serious danger; the curfew would not. We should reject the curfew.
questions.stem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the council member's reasoning?
choices: A rule should be rejected if there is no good reason to think that it would reduce the problem it is meant to address.
Accepting one restriction on a group of people does not commit anyone to accepting every other restriction on that group.
A restriction that shields people from serious danger to themselves is justified even if most of those restricted would never have been harmed.
A rule meant to address a problem should be rejected if some other means could reduce that problem without burdening anyone.
Restricting an entire group is justified only if it prevents substantial harm to others or guards that group against grave hazards.
questions.explanation: The member makes two points: the curfew prevents only minor harm to others, and, unlike a driving age, it doesn't protect young people from serious danger. (E) says restricting a whole group needs one of exactly those two justifications (preventing substantial harm to others or protecting the group from grave hazards), so the curfew, having neither, is unwarranted. (B) is the trap: it neutralizes the driving-age comparison but gives no reason to reject the curfew. (C) explains why the driving age is acceptable, not why the curfew isn't, and (A) is met, since the member concedes the curfew would cut vandalism.

So the right principle has to make both points matter: a restriction on a whole group is OK only if it prevents serious harm to others or protects the group itself. The curfew does neither, so reject. Watch for answers that handle just one front, or that answer the objection without ever telling you to reject.
